[1. Method of Rājayoga][I. Method of Rājayoga] \phantomsection Homage to the glorious GaṇeśaGanesa@Gaṇeśa. 1.5em Now, the method of RājayogaRajayoga@Rājayoga is laid down. 1.5em This is the fruit of RājayogaRajayoga@Rājayoga!definition: Through Rājayoga, the long term durability of the body arises even when there is the manifold enjoyment of political power [and] even when there is manifold royal entertainment and spectacle.Rajayoga@Rājayoga!wealth and sensual pleasuresThis unique definition of Rājayoga hints at an exceptionally wealthy lifestyle of Rāmacandra'sRamacandra@Rāmacandra audience.Tattvayogabindu@Tattvayogabindu!intended audienceThat alone is Rājayoga. 1.5em These are the varieties [of Rājayoga]:yoga taxonomy 1.5em 1. KriyāyogaKriyayoga@Kriyāyoga (``Yoga of [mental] action''); 2. JñānayogaJnanayoga@Jñānayoga (``Yoga of gnosis''); 3. CaryāyogaCaryayoga@Caryāyoga (``Yoga of conduct'');The first three yogas invite comparison with the familiar ŚaivaSaivism@Śaivism categories of kriyākriya@kriyā, caryācarya@caryā, jñānajnana@jñāna, and yogayoga@yoga; cf. nisvasa2015.4. HaṭhayogaHathayoga@Haṭhayoga (``Yoga of force''); 5. KarmayogaKarmayoga (``Yoga of deeds''); 6. LayayogaLayayoga (``Yoga of absorption''); 7. DhyānayogaDhyanayoga@Dhyānayoga (``Yoga of meditation''); 8. MantrayogaMantrayoga (``Yoga of mantra''); 9. LakṣyayogaLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga (``Yoga of foci''); 10. VāsanāyogaVasanayoga@Vāsanāyoga (``Yoga of mental residues''); 11. ŚivayogaSivayoga@Śivayoga (``Yoga of Śiva''); 12. BrahmayogaBrahmayoga (``Yoga of Brahman''); 13. AdvaitayogaAdvaitayoga (``Yoga of non duality''); 14. SiddhayogaSiddhayoga (``Yoga of the Siddhas''); 15. RājayogaRajayoga@Rājayoga!yoga for kings (``Yoga for kings'').For this meaning of Rājayoga, see birch2014.These are the fifteen yogas.The definitive source of the list of the fifteen yogas presented at the beginning of the text is uncertain. Rāmacandra's text is largely based on the content and structure of the YogasvarodayaYogasvarodaya@Yogasvarodaya (YSv) as quoted in ramatosana (Ed. pp. 831–858). In this text, however, the list is incomplete. YSv mentions a total of fifteen yogas but names only eight subcategories of Rājayoga. Rāmacandra may therefore have felt the need to complete the list. The other source he used for compiling his text is ssplonavlaSiddhasiddhantapaddhati@Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati (SSP), which does not present such a list. NārāyaṇatīrthaNarayanatirtha@Nārāyaṇatīrtha presents an almost identical list in his yogacandrikaYogacandrika@Yogacandrikā. A comparable list of twelve yogas occurs in Sundardās'sSundardas@Sundardās sarvangayogaSarvangayoga@Sarvāṅgayoga. A detailed investigation of the fifteen yogas is presented from p. onwards.\flushpage

div.head: [2. Characteristics of Kriyāyoga]
div.note: [II. Characteristics of Kriyāyoga]

\indent Now, the characteristic of KriyāyogaKriyayoga@Kriyāyoga!characteristics is described.For a comparative analysis of the various forms of Kriyāyoga in texts containing complex yoga taxonomiesyoga taxonomy, see p.~ et seqq.The most famous mention of the term kriyāyoga appears in PātañjalayogaśāstraPatanjalayogasastra@Pātañjalayogaśāstra or YogasūtraYogasutra@Yogasūtra 2.1 where it is defined as: tapaḥsvādhyāyeśvarapraṇidhānāni kriyāyogaḥ || 2.1 || See yogasutra. According to the introduction of this sūtra in the VyāsabhāṣyaVyasabhasya@Vyāsabhāṣya, KriyāyogaKriyayoga@Kriyāyoga!Pātañjali is presented as a means by which someone with a distracted mind can attain yoga (vyutthitacitto 'pi yogayuktaḥ). Yoga, which for PatañjaliPatanjali@Patañjali is samādhisamadhi@samādhi, shall be achieved by the three elements of Kriyāyoga, namely mental, moral, and physical austerity (tapastapas@tapas), repetition of mantrasmantra@mantra or study of sacred literature (svadhyāyasvadhyaya@svadhyāya) and surrender to god (īśvarapraṇidhānaisvarapranidhana@īśvarapraṇidhāna). This trinity of means is supposed to destroy the impurities (kleśasklesa@kleśa) of cittacitta@citta. These are given in Pātanjalayogaśāstra 2.3 as ignorance (avidyāavidya@avidyā), egoism (asmitāasmita@asmitā), attachment (rāgaraga@rāga), aversion (dveṣadvesa@dveṣa) and the urge to live (abhiniveśaabhinivesa@abhiniveśa), see yogasutra. The three major terms of Patañjali's Kriyāyoga are absent in the TattvayogabinduTattvayogabindu@Tattvayogabindu. Nevertheless, the individual elements of the kleśas, along with the aim to reduce these in the yogi's mind, can also be found in the Tattvayogabindu. In his commentary on the Pātanjalayogaśāstra, titled YogasiddhāntacandrikāYogasiddhantacandrika@Yogasiddhāntacandrikā, NārāyaṇatīrthaNarayanatirtha@Nārāyaṇatīrtha, who, like RāmacandraRamacandra@Rāmacandra, uses a very similar list of fifteen yogas, presents Kriyāyoga as the first item on his list and explains its purpose as the generation of samādhi and the reduction of kleśas, cf. yogacandrika.2.1 This yoga is liberation through [mental] action. It bestows success (siddhisiddhi@siddhi) in one's own body. Whatever wave the mind creates at the commencement of an action, through constantly restraining that very [wave] Kriyāyoga arises.
2.2 Patience, discrimination, equanimity, peace, modesty, desirelessness:Kriyayoga@Kriyāyoga!positive mental qualities the one endowed with these means is said to be a KriyāyogīKriyayogi@Kriyāyogī.
2.3 Envy, selfishness, cheating, violence, expectation, intoxication and pride, lust, anger, fear, laziness, greed, error, and impurity,~\ldots
2.4 \ldots ~attachment and aversion, disgust and laziness, error, deceit, envy and confusion:Kriyayoga@Kriyāyoga!negative mental qualities Whoever does not experience these is called a Kriyāyogī.

div.note: 1.5em In whose mind ``patience, discrimination, equanimity, peace, contentment'', etc., are cultivated without interruption, he alone is called a Yogī of many actions (bahukriyāyogībahukriyayogi@bahukriyāyogī).The term bahukriyāyogībahukriyayogi@bahukriyāyogī (``yogī of many actions'') occurs solely in the TattvayogabinduTattvayogabindu@Tattvayogabindu. Both the YogasvarodayaYogasvarodaya@Yogasvarodaya and the YogasaṃgrahaYogasamgraha@Yogasaṃgraha use only kriyāyogīKriyayogi@Kriyāyogī in their discussions of KriyāyogaKriyayoga@Kriyāyoga. To my knowledge, bahukriyāyogī is otherwise unattested and thus likely a neologism coined by RāmacandraRamacandra@Rāmacandra to emphasise the multitude of negative mental fluctuations to be restrained and positive ones to be cultivated by the kriyāyogī.Kriyayoga@Kriyāyoga!mental disciplineFraud, the state of being deceptive, violence, craving, envy, ego, anger, fear, shame, greed, delusion, impurity, attachment, aversion, laziness, heterodoxy, error, agitation of the senses, sexual desire: He in whose inner organIn Tattvayogabindu 51 (Ed. p. ), Rāmacandra's inner organ (antaḥkaraṇaantahkarana@antaḥkaraṇa) consists of mind (manasmanas@manas), intellect (buddhibuddhi@buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāraahamkara@ahaṃkāra), mental faculty (cittacitta@citta) and consciousness (caitanyacaitanya@caitanya).these diminish from day to day, he alone is called a Yogī of many actions (bahukriyāyogī).\phantomsection

div.head: [3. Varieties of Rājayoga]
div.p: [III. Varieties of Rājayoga]
div.note: Now, varieties of RājayogaRajayoga@Rājayoga are described. What are they? One is Si\ ddha\ ku\ ṇḍa\ li\ nī\ yo\ gaSiddhakundaliniyoga@Siddhakuṇḍalinīyoga [and one is] MantrayogaMantrayoga.The use of the term siddhakuṇḍalinīyogaSiddhakundaliniyoga@Siddhakuṇḍalinīyoga instead of siddhayogaSiddhayoga as listed initially is striking. Furthermore, this type of yoga, presented as the second last item in the initial yoga taxonomyyoga taxonomy (TYB 1, p. ), is introduced as the second type right after KriyāyogaKriyayoga@Kriyāyoga, the first item in both the initial list and the subsequent text. That raises further questions as the term kuṇḍaliṇīKundalini@Kuṇḍalinī is not mentioned in the subsequent description. However, in choosing this formulation, RāmacandraRamacandra@Rāmacandra probably had in mind the ascent of the KuṇḍalinīKundalini@Kuṇḍalinī through the nine cakrascakra@cakracakra@cakra!ninefold system he presented (see p. , n. ). The relation between SiddhakuṇḍalinīyogaSiddhakundaliniyoga@SiddhakuṇḍalinīyogaSiddhakundaliniyoga@Siddhakuṇḍalinīyoga!relation to Mantrayoga and MantrayogaMantrayogaMantrayoga!relation to Siddhakuṇḍalinīyoga appears mysterious since only witness U2 describes a specific type of Mantrayoga. The additional passages of witness U2, marked in greyscale, instruct the ``recitation of the non recitation'' (ajapājapaajapajapa@ajapājapa) of the haṃsamantrahamsamantra@haṃsamantra, also called ajapāgāyatrīajapagayatri@ajapāgāyatrī, during meditation for almost every (seven out of nine) cakra. All witnesses except L (L omits mantrayoga) preserve this reading, and the sentence following supports the reading of mantrayoga by dual forms. The TattvayogabinduTattvayogabindu@Tattvayogabindu closely follows the structure of the YogasvarodayaYogasvarodaya@Yogasvarodaya, as quoted in PrāṇatoṣiṇīPranatosini@Prāṇatoṣiṇī and YogakarṇikāYogakarnika@Yogakarṇikā. However, the yoga introduced there is jñānayogaJnanayoga@Jñānayoga and neither siddhakuṇḍalinīyoga nor mantrayoga are mentioned. The saradaavalon 25.37ab, however, provides a possible and plausible explanation: bibharti kuṇḍalī śaktir ātmānaṃ haṃsaṃ āśritā | ``The kuṇḍalīkundali@kuṇḍalī ŚaktiSakti@Śakti abides in the haṃsaḥhamsa@haṃsaḥ [and] supports the [individual] Self.'' See saradatilakafull.\phantomsection \flushpage

div.p: cf. YSv (PT, p. 831): paṭhanāt smaraṇād vyānān maṇḍanāt brahmasādhakaḥ | tad bhedasyaikasandhānam aṣṭaiśvaryamayo bhavet | tritīrthaṃ yatra nāḍī ca tripuṇyaṃ parameśvari | \ldots eṣo 'sya viśvarūpasya rājayogo mato budhaiḥ | viśeṣaṃ kathayiṣyāmi śṛṇu caikamanāḥ sati | mūlakande sthale caikā nāḍī tejasvatī parā (tejasvitāparā YK 1.246) | gudorddhe (gudordhve YK 1.247) sā tribhāgābhūd iḍā (tridhā bhūyād iḍā vāme YK 1.247) nāma śaśiprabhā | śaktirūpā mahānāḍī dhyānāt sarvārthadāyinī | dakṣiṇe 'pi kulākhyeti (dakṣiṇe piṅgalākhyeti YK 1.248) puṃrūpā sūryavigrahā | madhyabhāge suṣumnākhyā brahmaviṣṇuśivātmikā | śuddhacittena sā vijñā vidyutkoṭisamaprabhā | bhuktimuktipradā dhyānād aṇimādiguṇapradā | suṣumnāntaḥ samāśritya navacakraṃ yathā śṛṇu | mūlādhāraṃ catuṣpatraṃ gudorddhe (gudordhve YK 1.250) varttate mahat \approx Yogasaṃgraha (IGNCA 30020, f. 2v. ll. 3–7): mūlakandasthāne ekā tejomayā mahānāḍī vartate | iyaṃ iḍāpiṅgalasuṣumnā bhedā tridhā | vāma\ bhāge candrarūpā iḍā | dakṣiṇabhāge sūryarūpā piṅgalā | madhyamārge atisūkṣmā visataṃtusamākārā koṭividyutprabhā bhuktimuktipradā suṣumnā nāḍī vartate | yasyāḥ jñāne puruṣaḥ sarvajño bhavati | atas taj jñānotpattāv upāyā ucyaṃte | gudamūlacakraṃ caturdalaṃ | 1excf. div.note: These two RājayogasRajayoga@Rājayoga are described [in the following].See p.~ et seqq. for SiddhakuṇḍalinīyogaSiddhakundaliniyoga@Siddhakuṇḍalinīyoga and p.~ et seqq. for MantrayogaMantrayoga.In the location of the root bulbThe kandakanda@kanda (``bulb'') in yogic literature is usually below the navel or near the perineum. It seems that Rāmacandra'sRamacandra@Rāmacandra concept of the kanda is close to the one found in vivekamartandaoldaVivekamartanda@Vivekamārtaṇḍa 16: ūrdhvaṃ meḍhrād adho nābheḥ kandayoniḥ khagāṇḍavat | tatra nāḍyaḥ samutpannāḥ sahasrāṇi dvisaptatiḥ || ``Above the penis and below the navel is the home of the kanda, which is [formed] like the egg of a bird. There, the 72000 channels originate.''exists one major channelnadi@nāḍī in the form of light. This one channel splits up into Iḍāida@Iḍā, Piṅgalāpingala@Piṅgalā and Suṣumnāsusumna@Suṣumnā.nadi@nāḍī!three principal channels On the left side is the lunar Iḍā channel. On the right side exists the solar Piṅgalā channel. Within the middle path, having the very subtle form equal to the fibre of a lotus stalk [and] shining like a thousand lightnings, bestowing enjoyment and liberation, [and] having the form of benevolence,The expression śivarūpiṇī suṣumṇānāḍī derives from the source passage suṣumnākhyā brahmaviṣṇuśivātmikā in the YogasvarodayaYogasvarodaya@Yogasvarodaya, where suṣumṇā is described as having ``the nature of BrahmāBrahma@Brahmā, ViṣṇuVisnu@Viṣṇu, and ŚivaSiva@Śiva''. Rāmacandra omits the first two and instead attributes to the suṣumṇānāḍīsusumnanadi@suṣumṇānāḍī a specifically ``Śiva form'', associated with benevolence and auspiciousness, the precise meaning of which remains open to interpretation.the central channel occurs.The decision to adopt the reading śivarūpiṇī suṣumṇānāḍī pravartate, attested only in U2, is not without problems, yet preferable for several reasons. Without it, the sentence remains syntactically incomplete and semantically opaque, and the referent of asyā in the following sentence is unclear — especially since iḍā and piṅgalā have already been introduced, so the omission of suṣumṇā, the most important of the three, would be unexpected. Although U2 elsewhere contains additional material on the nine cakrascakra@cakra — likely secondary — this case appears different, as it preserves a sentence seemingly lost very early in the rest of the tradition. This is supported by the Yogasvarodaya and the YogasaṃgrahaYogasamgraha@Yogasaṃgraha (bhuktimuktipradā suṣumnā nāḍī vartate). Stemmatic considerations likewise favour this choice, since the redactor or scribe of U2 likely had access to an exemplar close to the \gamma archetype.When the knowledge of her has arisen, the person becomes omniscient.

div.note: The first is the ādhāracakra.This term already occurs in the tenfold cakra system of the 13th c. samgitaratna 2.120ab.The location is the anus. The color is red. The deity is GaṇeśaGanesa@Gaṇeśa. The power is success and intelligence. The mount is a rat. The Ṛṣi is Kūrma. The seal is contraction. The vital wind is Apānaapana@Apāna. The digit is Ūrmi. The concentration is Ojasvinī. In the four petals [exist] rajas, sattva, tamas and the mind faculties; [as well as] vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ and saṃ. A trident is [situated] in the internal triangle. In its middle is kāmapīṭhaThis refers to one of the four pīṭhas of tantric Buddhism and the Kaula Yoginī Tantra named KāmarūpaKamarupa@Kāmarūpa, specifically the present day KāmākhyāKamakhya@Kāmākhyā Temple in Assam, which is identified with different parts of the yogic body in various traditions. For detailed discussions, see liersch2026, rosati2020, and asiddhi. The Śārṅgadharapaddhati, ŚivaSiva@Śivayogapradīpikā, and Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati (all teaching a ninefold cakra system) place Kāmarūpa at the brahmacakra.in the shape of a triangle. In the middle of this seat (pīṭha) exists a single manifestation in the shape of a flame of fire. As a result of meditation on this manifestation, all literature, [such as] śāstras, poetry, drama, etc., appears in the person's mind without learning. From this [arises] external bliss, yogic bliss, heroic bliss [and] the bliss of coming to rest.The 11th century Amanaska, the earliest text on RājayogaRajayoga@Rājayoga, already mentions various blisses such as ānanda, paramānanda, sahajānanda, and cinmātrānanda (birch2013). A similar group (paramānanda, sahajānanda, vīrānanda, yogānanda) is associated with the first cakra in the 13th century samgitaratna (2.120cd–2.121ab). Earlier references to the ``four blisses'' appear in Vajrayāna sexual yoga (see isaac2014; sferra2000), and the hevajra (1.1.28 et passim) lists ānanda, paramānanda, sahajānanda, and viramānanda, the latter referring to male pleasure at ejaculation. These concepts were adopted in the asiddhi, which, however, contrasts sexual ritual with a celibate yoga. It states that semen (bindu) is the source of ``the blisses whose last is Virama'' (7.4) and that accomplished yogins experience three blisses without ejaculation (34.3), reflecting its ascetic orientation (asiddhi). Later texts, including the Amaraughaprabodha, which cite the Amṛtasiddhi, modified or removed such Buddhist sexual yogic terminology (birch2019).A hundredfold recitation of the non recitation: 600. 1 ghaṭi [and] 40 palas.See p. n. for an explanation of the units of measurement. \flushpage

[5. Svādhiṣṭānacakra]
[V. Svādhiṣṭānacakra] \phantomsection 1mm Now, the second is the six petalled SvādhiṣṭhānacakraSvadhisthanacakra@Svādhiṣṭhānacakra known as the seat of UḍḍīyāṇaUddiyana@UḍḍīyāṇaThe term uḍḍīyāṇa originally refers to one of the four pīṭhas of tantric Buddhism and the Kaula Yoginī Tantra, see white1996. According to kowski1988 (1988), sandersonshaivaexe (2007) and urban2010 (2010), UḍḍiyānaUddiyana@Uḍḍīyāṇa is probably situated in the Swat Valley in modern Pakistan. See sandersonshaivaexe for a detailed term discussion. Throughout the text corpus of HaṭhayogaHathayoga@Haṭhayoga, the pīṭhas are repeatedly located differently in the yogic body.\phantomsection The location is the penis. The colour is yellow. The shine is yellow. The quality is Rajas. The deity is BrahmāBrahma@Brahmā. The speech is Vaikharī. The power is SāvitrīSavitri@Sāvitrī. The mount is the goose. The Ṛṣi is VaruṇaVaruna@Varuṇa. The light is the fire of passion. The body is gross. The state is waking. The Veda is Ṛg. The object of veneration (liṅga) is the teacher. The liberation is Brahmasalokatā.The term brahmasalokatā might be translated as ``residing in the world of Brahmā.''The principle is the pure state. The sense object is smell. The vital wind is Apānaapana@Apāna. The internal syllables [are]:In all instances where U2 provides the inner (antar°) syllables and outer (bahir°) mother goddesses, I have corrected and standardised all occurrences of °mātrā or °mātrāḥ to the appropriate word and form, which is °mātṛkāḥ. Thanks to James MallinsonMallinson, James for this suggestion. The emended form, °mātṛkāḥ, on the one hand, conveys a clearer meaning when applied to syllables placed on the cakras, while also signifying ``mothers'' or ``mother goddesses,'' precisely as presented in all cases where U2 provides bahirmātṛkā. In any case, U2 yields a list of goddesses in the nominative singular feminine. Furthermore, this decision is reinforced by evidence from other texts. See for example Agastyamuni's rajayoga (f. 8–9) which contains nearly identical syllable combinations that are placed on the petals of the cakras within its sixfold cakra system.vaṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ. The external mother goddesses [are]: Kāmā, KāmākhyāKamakhya@Kāmākhyā, Tejasvinī, Ceṣṭikā, Alasā [and] Mithunā.The worship of mothers is originally a central element of the Śākta tradition known as Kaula Śaivism. It belongs to the Mantramārga and developed from the former Kāpālika cult. See oberlies2012.A thousandfold recitation of the non recitation; 6000; 16 ghaṭis [and] 40 palas. In its middle exists an extremely red light. The adept becomes very handsome as a result of meditation on it. He becomes one whom young women desire. His lifespan increases every day. \flushpage

[6. Lotus within the place of the navel]
[VI. Lotus within the place of the navel] \phantomsection The third lotus exists at the location of the navelcakra@cakra!navelThe important mention of kuṇḍalinī in SSP 2.3 (Ed. p. 30) and a parallel passage in Nāḍīcakra scroll (ORIS 1334, ll. 155–163) are discussed on p. .[and] has ten petals. The color is reddish. The deity is ViṣṇuVisnu@Viṣṇu. The power is LakṣmīLaksmi@Lakṣmī. The Ṛṣi is Āyu.The name vayu for a ṛṣi as attested in manuscript U2 is probably a mistake. Since immediately afterwards, the associated vāyu is given, this should be an eyeskip. My best guess is āyu, the name of a sage mentioned in rigveda 2.14.7 and geldner1907.The vital wind is Samānasamana@Samāna. The mount is GaruḍaGaruda@Garuḍa. The body is the subtle body.I corrected devatāha to dehaḥ since a deity has already been mentioned before, sūkṣmaliṅgaṃ most likely refers to a deha and, as in the second cakra the deha is followed by an avasthā.The state is sleep. The speech is MadhyamāMadhyama@Madhyamā. The Veda is Yajur[veda]. The fire is the southern [fire]. The liberation is Samīpatā. The guruliṅgaFor the phallus of ŚivaSiva@Śiva, considered as one’s teacher or guide, cf. shivapura 1.18.31.is Viṣṇu. The principle is water. The sense object is taste.I emended rajo to raso since the association of water with taste is well known.There are ten petals [and] ten mātṛkās. [The] internal syllables [are]: ḍaṃ ṭaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ. The external mother goddesses [are]: Śānti, Kṣamā, Medhā, Tanayā, Medhāvinī, Puṣkarā, Haṃsagamanā, Lakṣyā, Tanmayā and Amṛtā.I was unable to locate parallel lists of bahirmātṛkāḥ for the navel cakra in other sources, and a comprehensive search of my electronic text library yielded no occurrences. The association of deities with cakra petals or syllable series is, however, well attested for instance in the RudraRudrayāmala Uttaratantra with antecedents traceable to the kubji1988, albeit with differing enumerations. The pairing of antarmātṛkānyāsa and bahirmātṛkānyāsa, denoting the implantation of syllables within the cakras and their reinforcement on the outer body, is widespread and further elaborated in works such as the Dīpikā on the Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava and the Śāradātilaka. I am grateful to Shaman HatleyHatley, Shaman for discussing this topic with me.A thousandfold recitation of the non recitation; 6000; 16 ghaṭis [and] 40 palas.Thus, the prescribed duration for meditation on this cakra is six hours and forty minutes.Unlike the preceding svādhiṣṭhānacakraṃ this cakra at the navel is not associated with a guṇa, a dhāraṇā, a prabhā and a mudrā.In its middle exists a cakra with five angles. In the middle of it is a single manifestation. It is not possible to describe the splendour of it with speech. \flushpage

div.note: As a result of meditation on this manifestation, the body of the person becomes durable.The source text specifies this bodily durability as a long lifespan (cirāyuḥ) and freedom from diseases (arogatā).

[7. Lotus within the heart]
[VII. Lotus within the Heart] \phantomsection The fourth lotus is twelve petalled [and] exists within the heart.cakra@cakra!heart The place of the AnāhatacakraAnahatacakra@AnāhatacakraThe designation aṣṭamam anāhatacakraṃ in the Nāḍīcakra (ORIS 1334, l. 97) for the cakra located in the heart — here referred to as anāhatacakra — is the result of a chain of scribal errors, confusions and conceptual extension. While the first two cakras in the Nāḍīcakra (ORIS 1334) largely correspond to witness U2, the Nāḍīcakra (ORIS 1334) refers to the third cakra as kuṇḍalinīsthānam without specifying its precise location, which is, however, indicated towards the end (l. 163) by the term garbhapuṭaṃ which is the womb below the navel. The fourth cakra in the Nāḍīcakra (ORIS 1334) is the Maṇipūracakra at the navel (ll. 142–154), corresponding to the third cakra in U2. The fifth cakra in the Nāḍīcakra (ORIS 1334) is the Manacakra, the description of which appears in U2 within the account of the heart cakra. Subsequently, the Nāḍīcakra (ORIS 1334) identifies the heart cakra as the eighth (aṣṭamam), which, however, must be a scribal error for the original ṣaṣṭham, since the Viśuddhicakra, which follows (l. 79), is recorded as the seventh (saptamam), and yet another eighth cakra (ll. 68–69) is then listed at the site of the nose (nāsikāsthānam). Thereafter, three further cakras follow, which again correspond almost verbatim to the supplementary material preserved in U2.is at the heart. The colour is white. The quality is Tamas. The deity is RudraRudra. The power is UmāUma@Umā. The Ṛṣi is HiraṇyagarbhaHiranyagarbha@Hiraṇyagarbha. The mount is NandīNandi@Nandī. The vital wind is Prāṇaprana@Prāṇa. The body is the instrument of the digit of light. The state is deep sleep. The speech is PaśyantīPasyanti@Paśyantī. The Veda is Samā[veda]. The fire is the fire of the householder. The liṅga is ŚivaSiva@Śiva. The level is attaining.Cf. yogasutra 3.45: prāptir aṅgulyagreṇāpi spṛśati candramasam | ``Attaining is that by which one can touch the moon with the fingertips.''The liberation is taking the same form [as the deity]. [There are] twelve petals. [The] twelve [internal] syllables [are]: kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṇaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ. The external mother goddesses [are]: Rudrāṇī, Tejasā, Tāpinī, Sukhadā, Caitanyā, Śivadā, Śānti, Umā, Gaurī, Mātarā, Jvalā [and] Prajvālinī. A thousandfold recitation of the non recitation; 6000; 16 ghaṭis [and] 40 palas.

div.note: Because of being made of [such an] intense light, [the fourth lotus] is not in the range of sight. In its middle exists an eight petalled lotus facing downwards.For a discussion of the eight petalled lotus within the twelve petalled lotus in the heart, see p.~.The mind resides in the cakra. The deity is Manas. The power is Bahiś.Bahiśśaktiḥ is the external energy that permeates the external space. The conjecture is based on kriyakrama (Ed. p. 96) and sakalagama quoted with reference siddhāntaśekhare (Ed. p. 80): caraṇāṅguṣṭhayor yugmāt sañcintya suṣirāntanau | suṣirāntabahiśśaktiṃ vyāpinīṃ cintayet tataḥ || The reading attested in the parallel Nāḍīcakra, which developed within the same textual tradition, is buddhiśakti. While this cannot be entirely ruled out, given the poor quality of the transmission in the scroll, I strongly doubt that this reading is original.The Ṛṣi is the self. In the middle of the heartI conjectured nābhi° to hṛdaya° since the context is an eight petalled within the twelve petalled lotus whose eight petals are discussed in U2, cf. Tattvayogabindu 47.is a lotus whose stalk is ten fingers long. Its stalk is soft. [The lotus] is pure [and] facing downwards. There is [something] resembling a banana flower established within it. The mind wants advancement, but its essence is indecision. While the mind rests on the eastern petal, which is white, a clear intellect endowed with the fame of dharma, knowledge, etc., arises. While in the southeast, which is reddish, a mind endowed with weakness, illusion, sleepiness, and laziness arises. While in the right south, being black, the production of anger arises. While in the southwest, which is blue, a mind of selfishness arises. While in the west, which is brown, a mind [focussed on] play, laughter, and excitement arise. While in the northwest, which is dark in colour, a mind endowed with worry and anxiety arises. While in the north, which is yellow, a mind occupied with enjoyment, sexual passion, and prosperity arises. While in the northeast, which is whitish, a mind united with gnosis arises. \flushpage

div.note: It is said that in its middle is the place of the prāṇa vital wind [and] in the middle [of] the eight petalled lotus is a central receptacle (karṇikā)Regarding the translation of karṇikā as ``central receptacle'' instead of the widespread translation ``pericarp'', see reigle2012.in the form of a liṅga. The technical designation of it is bud (kalikā).A similar concept, including the usage of the term kalikā, is found in the chapter on creation (sargakāṇḍa) of the ramatosana. In a quotation attributed to a text called Śāktānanda, the jīva is described as having the shape of a bud of light (pradīpakalikākāro jīvo) and always resides in the heart: ādau sañjāyate bījaṃ brahmāṇḍaṃ sahasāṅkuraḥ | tasya madhye sumeruś ca kaṅkāladaṇḍarūpadhṛk | carācarāṇāṃ sarveṣāṃ devādīnāṃ viśeṣataḥ | ālayaḥ savabhūtānāṃ meror abhyantare 'pi ca | pradīpakalikākāro jīvo hṛdi sadā sthitaḥ |In the middle of this bud exists a single thumb sized [divine] figurine (puttalikā)The concept of a puttalikā in the heart can be traced back to the Kaula Tantras, e.g., the saradaavalon 22.126–128: puttalikāyā hṛdayaṃ spṛśan prāṇā iha prāṇā jīva iha sthita iti indriyāṇi spṛśan sarvendriyāṇi vāṅmanaścakṣuḥśrotraghrāṇeti sarvāṅgaṃ spṛśan prāṇā ihāyāntu sukhaṃ ciraṃ tiṣṭhan tu iti śiraḥ spṛśan svāheti japet | mantranyāsam iti |being similar to a ruby gem in color. Her technical designation is JīvaJiva@Jīva.The idea of the thumb sized soul residing in the heart is already present in the oldest strata of yogic literature. See kathaup 6.17: aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ puruṣo 'ntarātmā sadā janānāṃ hṛdaye saṃniviṣṭaḥ | taṃ svāc charīrāt pravṛhen muñjād iveṣīkāṃ dhairyeṇa | taṃ vidyāc chukram amṛtaṃ taṃ vidyāc chukram amṛtam iti || Also cf. Śvetāśvataropaniṣadhauschild1927 3.13: aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ puruṣo 'ntarātmā sadā janānāṃ hṛdaye sanniviṣṭaḥ | hṛdā manīṣā manasābhikḷpto ya etad vidur amṛtās te bhavanti ||Not even with ten million tongues is it possible to talk about her nature and her power. As a result of meditation on this form, the women of the inhabitants of the world [which are] Humans, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Guhyakas, Vidyādharas, in the heavenly world, underworld, and open space become obedient to the will of the practising person. What [more] is here to say about this? \flushpage

[8. Lotus within the location of the throat]
[VIII. Lotus within the location of the throat] \phantomsection Now, the fifth sixteen petalled lotus exists at the location of the throat.cakra@cakra!throat The color is grey. The deity is JīvaJiva@Jīva. The power is ignorance. The Ṛṣi is Virāṭa. The mount is the vital wind. The vital wind is Udānaudana@Udāna. The digit is the flame. The lock is JālandharaJalandhara@Jālandhara. The body is the primordial cause (mahākāraṇa). The state is the fourth state (tūrya). The speech is ParāPara@Parā. The Veda is Atharvaṇa[veda]. The object of veneration is the movable. The level is Jīvaprāptā. The liberation is the union with the deity (sāyujyatā). [Associated with it are] sixteen petals [and] sixteen mother goddesses (mātṛkas). The internal syllables [are]: aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ \newfontfamily Adobe Text Pro\adobetextpro ṝṃ ḷṃ \adobetextpro ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aṃḥ. The external mother goddesses [are]: Vidyā, Avidyā, Icchā, Śakti, Jñānaśakti, Śatalā, Mahāvidyā, Mahāmayā, Buddhi, Tāmasī, Maitrā, Kumārī, Maitrāyaṇī, Rudrā, Puṣṭā, Siṃhanī. A thousandfold recitation of the non recitation; 1000; 2 ghaṭis, 46 palas. 40 akṣaras. In its middle exists the one consciousnessThe term puruṣa appears in the last three sentences of this section. Judging by the context, puruṣa in the first two sentences must be understood as ``consciousness'', perhaps with the same connotations as in the Sāṃkhya Yoga traditions. In contrast, the sentence concluding the section must refer to the person practising meditation.shining like a thousand moons. As a result of meditation on this consciousness, incurable diseases vanish. The person lives up to 1001 years.

[9. ĀjñācakraAjnacakra@Ājñācakra]\phantomsection
[IX. Ājñācakra] Now, a sixthInterestingly, the scroll entitled Nāḍīcakra (ORIS 1334, ll. 68–77), which is situated in the same textual tradition as the supplementary material preserved in witness U2, inserts immediately prior to the Ājñācakra located between the eyebrows an additional, eighth cakra positioned at the nose: oṃ aṣṭamaṃ balavāñ cakraṃ nāsikāsthānaṃ oṃkāro devatā svaṣamṇā śaktiḥ virāṭ ṛṣiḥ trivarṇata tridala 3 trimātrā 3 akāra ukāra makāra satvoguṇa rajoguṇa tamoguṇa brahmaviṣṇurudraḥ pṛthvī āpaḥ tejo vāyuḥ ākāśaḥ 5 prāṇa 'pāna vyāna dāna samāna 5 śabda sparśa rūpa rasa gandhaḥ 5 nāga kūrma kṛkala deva datta dhanañjaya 5 mano buddhi cittā antākaraṇa ahaṅkaraḥ 5 iḍā piṅgalā suṣuṃṇā.cakra named ĀjñāAjnacakra@Ājñācakra exists.Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati 2.7 declares this cakra to be thumb sized and calls it the eye of wisdom (jñānanetram) on which the practitioner is to meditate as a flame of a lamp thereby attaining perfection of speech: saptamaṃ bhrūcakraṃ madhyamāṅguṣṭhamātram | tatra jñānanetraṃ dīpaśikhākāraṃ dhyāyet | tatra vāksiddhir bhavati |The deity is fire. The power is the central channel. The Ṛṣi is Haṃsa. The mount is consciousness. The body is knowledge. The state is insight. The speech is the incomparable. The Veda is Samā[veda]. The object of veneration is intoxication. [It is consisting of] half a measure.It is difficult to make sense of ardhamātrā. My best guess is that an ardha divides something into two. It may be a synonymous expression referring to the two mātṛkas that follow.The principle is space. The gander is the living soul. The origin is the activity of consciousness. There are two māṭrkas. The inner syllables [are]: haṃ [and] kṣam. The external mother goddesses [are]: Sthiti [and] Prabhā. A thousandfold recitation of the non recitation; 1000; 2 ghaṭis, 46 palas, and 40 akṣaras. This two petalled cakra is in the middle of the eyebrows. In its middle exists a certain object in the form of a blazing fire without parts. [It is] not female, [it is] not male. As a result of meditation on it, the body of the person becomes non ageing and immortal. \flushpage

[10. Cakra within the palate]\phantomsection
[X. Cakra within the palate] Now, the seventh cakra, having sixty four petals [and] being full of nectar, exists in the middle of the palate.cakra@cakra!palateThe tālucakra follows the ājñācakra between the eyebrows, deviating from the usual ascending sequence. RāmacandraRamacandra@Rāmacandra adopts this order from the Yogasvarodaya (cf. table 19 in powell2023) but revises it in his second ninefold system in Tattvayogabindu 29 (p.~), following the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati, which places the tālucakra before the ājñācakra.The Maṇḍala is the forehead.The scribe of U2 likely altered the sentence to fit Rāmacandra’s cakra system. The reading lalāṭamaṇḍale in the Nāḍīcakra scroll (ORIS 1334) is preferable, as the cakra is located at the forehead rather than the palate. Rāmacandra’s deviation from the expected ascending sequence may thus reflect a conflation of different interpretive traditions.The deity is the moon. The power is the nectar of immortality. The Ṛṣi is the supreme self. The seventeenth digit is the residence of the nectar of immortality. [It is] the river that has waves consisting of nectar of immortality. [It is] the great space. [It is] the ``little mum''The terms aṃbikā, laṃbikā, ghaṇṭikā, and tālikā may refer to the uvula. In the jogpradipyaka, the haṭhayogic practice called manthana has two variations, see mallinson2010. The second type (vv. 643–653) instructs the yogin to use a metal peg (kīla dhātamaya) to churn, purify, and produce amī (= amṛta) at four locations: ambikā (frenum), lambikā (tongue), tālu (palate), and ghaṇṭikā (uvula). These places correspond to the teats of Kāmadhenu, the ``wish fulfilling cow'' (v. 651). The Vairāṭapurāṇa locates an amṛtacakra at the forehead emitting ``nectar''. That is the dwelling place of the gāyatrī, known as Kāmadhenu, with four teats: Ambikā, Lambikā, Ghaṇṭikā, and Tālikā, see kaviraj.[It is] the uvula. [It is] the TālikāThe precise meaning of tālikā is unclear. In a private correspondence (November 2023), mallinson2014b suggested it might originate from tālu.. [It is] the ``little bell''. The unspeakable Gāyatrī is the own form of [its] body.Tantric mantras are often associated with a deity and their bodies, see haasgayatri.Crow beaked, human eyedThe concept of ``human eyes'' probably emphasises the contrast with the traditional notion of crows possessing only a single eye. Thanks to Dr. Dominic A. haasgayatri for this hint., cow horned forehead, reciting the Brahman,Possibly the Veda or any sacred word, like i.e. the sacred syllable oṃ or speculatively even the ajapāgāyatrī itself. However, whether the haṃsa mantra is considered a Vedic Brahman is unclear. I am grateful for Dr. Dominic A. haasgayatri suggestions regarding this passage.horse necked, peacock faced [and] swan limbed is the own form of the unspeakable Gayatrī.The bird like body of the ajapāgāyatrī refers to the body of a particular haṃsa (``swan''), \ldots \flushpage

div.note: 2.2em since the ajapāgayatrī contains the unrecited [a]haṃ sa ``I am that'' expression. The haṃsa is a common metaphor for the soul wandering in the wheel of Brahman or Saṃsāra, cf. hauschild1927 1.6 and 3.18. The animal parts may symbolise the various physical embodiments which the jīva undergoes as it passes through the brahmacakra. The manuscript nadicakra (ORIS 1334) contains an illustration of the dehasvarūpa of ajapāgāyatrī. The text surrounding the illustration is almost identical to the description of U2 found here. See p.~ for the facsimile with the illustration. Furthermore, haasgayatri notes that while the association between the Vedic Gāyatrī and birds was once prominent in Vedic literature, it seems to have diminished. Here, however, it has survived in the context of the ajapāgāyatrī. Furthermore, in the Nāḍīcakra scroll (ORIS 1334), between the description of the ninth ĀjñācakraAjnacakra@Ājñācakra (ll. 58–67) and that of the subsequent tenth cakra (ll. 49–52), there appears an additional passage describing the Suṣumṇā (ll. 53–57): oṃ tejomayī nāḍī suṣumṇā madhyagāmṛtā yasyā mitaṃ idaṃ viśvaṃ proktaṃ ca puṭataṇḍavayogibhis tat praya 'nena jñeyā sā dehavarttinī tāṃ na jānanti ye mūḍhāḥ vṛthā te bhāravāhakāḥ tasyādidaṃ cakraṃ dhyeyaṃ jñeyaṃ ca vijñātamaiḥ.[It is] endowed with superabundant beauty. [It is] very bright. In its middle exists a unique central receptacle named ``the little bell'' (ghāṇṭikā)The term ghaṇṭikā, meaning ``little bell,'' commonly denotes the uvula, see mallinson2010 and padoux1994. Within the sixfold cakra system of kubji1988 7.85, the uvula serves as a pathway for the ascent of breath, mantra, and self between the fifth and the sixth cakra: lalanāghaṇṭike yojya pañcamaṃ sthānam ākramet | ākramed guhyacakraṃ tu karaṇaṃ cordhvamūlakam ||being red in colour. In its centre is a site. In the middle of that exists the hidden digit of the moon, which is oozing a stream of nectar. As a result of meditation on this digit, death does not go near him. As a result of uninterrupted meditation, the stream of nectar flows. Then, the states of wasting[ disease] (kṣayaroga),A fever that causes bodily depletion, cf. ayurveda, ayurveda.bilious fever (pittajvara),A fever due to disordered bile, cf. ibid. ayurveda.burning sensation of the heart (hṛdayadāha),The burning sensation in the heart caused by heart disease resulting from disordered bile, cf. ibid. ayurveda.head disease (śiroroga),The term refers to disorders of the head. When blood, fat, phlegm, or vata decreases, severe pain results; cf. ibid. ayurveda.and tongue insensibility (jihvājāḍya)Stiffness or numbness of the tongue, cf. ibid. ayurveda.vanish. Even ingested venom does not trouble if the mind is fixed on it. \flushpage

[11. Eighth cakra at the aperture of brahman]
[XI. Eighth cakra at the aperture of brahman] \phantomsection Now, [there] exists the eighth cakra having one hundred petals at the location of the aperture of Brahman.cakra@cakra!brahmarandhraThe brahmarandhra, often termed the ``aperture of Brahman,'' is a tiny opening at the crown near the fontanelle. Its name originates from ancient Upaniṣadic beliefs, portraying it as a portal for the individual soul (ātman) to surpass bodily limitations and merge with the absolute (brahman).The deity is the teacher. The power is consciousness. The Ṛṣi is Virāṭa.The Ṛṣi Virāṭa was previously assigned to the fifth cakra.[It is] the witness above everything. The nature of consciousness is the state beyond the fourth state. [It has] all colours. [It has] all mātrās.This could refer either to syllables or to mother goddesses, or to both.[It has] all petals. The body is Virāṭa.Due to the previously mentioned assignment of virāṭa to the Ṛṣi of the cakra, this could be an eyeskip, so that the originally intended assignment of the deha of the eighth cakra would be lost.The state is steady.Possibly in the sense of cessation.The speech is wisdom. The Veda is the ``I am that'' [expression] (so'haṃ). The place is unsurpassed. A thousandfold recitation of the non recitation; 1000; 2 ghaṭis, 46 palas, 40 akṣaras. The count of all mutterings [per day] is 21600. In this way, it carries on day and night. He who knows the breath is a learned person. 11.1 With the sound ``sa'', he exhales. With the sound ``ha'', he inhales again: ``I am he, he is I''. Because of that, the embodied soul constantly utters the Mantra.The exact source of this verse is unclear. Considering the possibilities presented in the parallels, it appears evident that this verse represents a mixed variant. It is likely that this verse was widespread in the yoga traditions of the time and was transmitted from text to text and orally from teacher to student, which may have led to the continual emergence of new variants.The supplementary material in U2 on this cakra terminates at this point, whereas the Nāḍīcakra scroll (ORIS 1334) transmits a slightly longer passage. Immediately following the verse, it reads (diplomatically transcribed): ādhare liṅganabhau hṛdaya sarasi je tālamūle lalāṭe dvīpatre śoḍaśāre dvidaśadaśadale dvādaśāre catuṣkayāsānte bālamadhye ḍapha kaṭa sahite kaṇṭhadeśe svarāṇāṃ haṃ kam tatvārthayuktaṃ sakaladalayutaṃ varṇarūpaṃ namāmi. This passage \ldots \flushpage

div.note: 2.2em constitutes a highly corrupt and partially difficult to reconstruct doxographical enumeration of localisations, presented in ascending order and occasionally accompanied by iconographic features such as the number of petals or phonetic elements. ``The seat of JālandharaJalandhara@Jālandhara'' is the name of its lotus.For a similar concept of Jālandhara see the description of the eighth cakra in saubhagya and ssplonavla 2.8.[It is] the place of the accomplished person. In the middle of it, there is a streak that looks like the manifestation of smoke and fire, and in such a way, the unique manifestation of consciousness exists. It has no end nor a beginning. As a result of meditation on the manifestation, direct perception of both the coming and going of the soul in space arises. Affliction from the earth element does not arise [anymore] even if one is within the earth.The meditation effect described here is probably an allusion to a yogic practice usually referred to in Hindi as bhūmigat samādhi. Through a trance like state of samādhi, certain yogis enable themselves to be buried underground for an extended period of time without suffering any lasting damage. See mallinson2010 and rootsofyoga2017 for more details on the practice and historical accounts. Biological studies have even been conducted to better understand the mechanisms of the human body that underlie this practice. See hypo.One constantly sees everything directly [and] one becomes separate.Probably ``separate from the rest of matter'' in the Sāṃkhya Yoga sense.The span of life increases significantly. \flushpage

[12. Cakra of the great void]
[XII. Cakra of the great void] \phantomsection Now, the divisions of the ninth cakra are explained.Other texts incorporate systems of nine places. For example kumbhaka 91–92, which presents a technique of kumbhaka for pratyāhāra: navasthānāni vijñāya pratyāhāraḥ sa vedhasaḥ | pādatalaguhyanābhihṛdayoraḥkaṇṭhagaṇṭikāḥ kramataḥ || 91 || bhrūmadhyaṃ ca lalāṭaṃ brahmasthānaṃ navaitāni | yogasiddhiḥ sarvaroganāśaḥ pratyāhṛtau bhavet || 92 || ``Having realised the nine places, this [following description] is the withdrawal of the senses according to the creator. Holding [the breath] in the sequence of [the following places] brings about success in yoga and destruction of all diseases: soles of the feet, generative organ, navel, heart, throat, uvula, middle of the eyebrows, forehead and the crown of the head''. In the goraksapaddhati 2.75–76 one finds nine places as dhyānasthānas, ``places for meditation'': gudaṃ meḍhraṃ ca nābhiś ca hṛtpadmaṃ ca tad ūrdhvataḥ | ghaṇṭikā laṃbikāsthāna bhrūmadhye ca nabhobilam || 75 || kathitāni navaitāni dhyānasthānāni yogibhiḥ |upādhitatvamuktāni kurvanty aṣṭaguṇodayam || 76 || ``Anus and generative organ and navel, heart and [the place] above [the heart], uvula, tongue, middle of eyebrows and crown of the head. These are the nine places of meditation [taught] by the yogis, freeing one from the material world's limitations and bestowing the eight supernatural powers.''Similar ninefold cakra systems can be identified in the Yogasvarodaya, the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati, and the Yogakarṇikā. Yet another text that presents a similar system and most likely quoted the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati without reference but with several redactions is the saubhagya.The designation of it is ``the cakra of the great void''.Mahasunyacakra@Mahāśūnyacakracakra@cakra!great void Above that, there is no other. Therefore, it is declared the ``the great accomplished cakra''. [Another] such name is ``[divine] seat of Pūrṇagiri''. In the middle of that mahāśūnyacakra exists a single upward facing extremely red thousand petalled lotus an abode of absolute splendour full of countless blessings, whose fragrance is not in range of mind [and] speech, [and] in the centre of this lotus exists one central receptacle in the shape of a triangle. \flushpage

div.note: In the middle of that central receptacle exists the seventeenth digit in an untainted form. The splendour of the digit is shining like ten million suns, but there is no occurrence of heat. Its coolness is that of ten million moons, and yet there is no occurrence of cold. As a result of meditation upon the digit, suffering does not arise in the practitioner's mind. Here, at this location the deity is ``I''(aham). The power is the ``he is I'' (so'ham). The Ṛṣi is the self. The path is the liberation. Above Brahma[randhra?]It is unclear whether this brahmordhvam signifies Brahman, BrahmāBrahma@Brahmā or even the brahmarandhra cakra. Since the syllable ``sa'' is situated in the agnicakra this location here could point at the upper part of the body, the point up to which the haṃ part of the breath ascends on inhalation.is haṃ.The syllable ``haṃ'' in this context refers to the first syllable of the word haṃsa.Haṃ is in the cakra.This particular cakra must refer to the current cakra which is described here, which appears to be the exact topmost point to which the breath ascends.In the cakra of fireSince the bodily fire in most texts of yoga is situated in the navel area, the agnicakra perhaps refers to the lowest point in the body to which the breath descends.is the letter ``sa''. The breathing becomes developed [and] the soul ascends and descends. The place is the hiding place of existence. The colour is yellow. The splendour is the shine of ten million suns. The shine always arises. The deity is ŚivaSiva@Śiva. The power is primordial illusion. The state is the dissolution of the self into HaraEpiphet of Śiva, cf. for example hathatattvakaumudi 25.6.which is the unbroken sound that is not subject to sonic change having the nature of subtle sonic matter.The term nāda in Śaiva contexts can be taken as ``subtle sonic matter'', cf. tantrika3.The seal is Aghorā. Primordial illusion.Possibly a dittography of the mention of mūlamāyā a few lines above. The point of mentioning it here is not clear to me.The body is original matter. [It is] not within the range of mind and speech. [It is] without manifestation. [It is] without doubt. Absorption into meditation and dissolution is the goal without waves [and] without tarnish.The meaning of the cruxed passage could not be reconstructed and translated with certainty. The translation is provisional. The compound layadhyānasamādhi seems to be a dvandva compound of the collective unit of the three related terms. The compound could, however, also be dissolved as a tatpuruṣa and translated as ``absorption into meditation and dissolution'', which seems to provide a better sense. \flushpage

div.note: Above that is the place of infinite supreme bliss. In that [place], there exists the upper power (ūrdhvaśakti)Examining the primary source for the composition of RāmacandraRamacandra@Rāmacandra's account of the ninth cakra, found in the Yogasvarodaya (cf. sources), one might infer that the term ūrdhvaśakti is a corruption of the term tadūrddhvataḥ. However, the term and concept are validated by its occurrence in Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati 2.9 (cf. sources), which Rāmacandra must have consulted as well. The association of ūrdhvaśakti with a kalā is likely an innovation by Rāmacandra, as the ūrdhvaśakti of the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati is not explicitly identified as a kalā. Moreover, the kalā mentioned in the YSv is not designated as a śakti. Rāmacandra, therefore, amalgamates assertions from both sources in his interpretation.as a unique digit which has such a designation. As a result of meditation on this digit, whatever the person wants arises. Even though [one is] enjoying royal pleasures, amusing oneself amongst women and watching musical performances, the person's digit grows daily like the digit of the moon in the bright half of the month. His body is not affected by merit and sin. As a result of uninterrupted meditation [onto this digit], the ability to illuminate one's own nature arises. He sees even remote objects as if they were near.The final testimony from Yogasaṃgraha IGNCA 30020 references its source as Tattvajñānapradīpikā (cf. testimonia). After that, the manuscript paraphrases and quotes other yoga texts such as the Uttaragītā.\flushpage

[13. Lakṣyayoga]
[XIII. Lakṣyayoga] \phantomsection Now, LakṣyayogaLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga (``Yoga of foci''),The original reading of the yoga is likely lakṣyayogaLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga since it is attested across both the \beta and \gamma groups. This reading is supported by the usage in the ssplonavlaSiddhasiddhantapaddhati@Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati 2.26–32 and yogacandrikaYogacandrika@Yogacandrikā (Ed. p. 2). However, ramatosana (Ed. pp. 833–834) and yogakarnikaYogakarnika@Yogakarṇikā (Ed. pp. 23–24) as well as sarvangayogaSarvangayoga@Sarvāṅgayoga (Ed. pp. 104–105) use the term lakṣayoga, indicating that both designations were common. See p. for a detailed discussion of Lakṣyayoga.which is easily accomplished,The emphasis on the ease of Lakṣ(y)ayoga is not just shared with the YogasvarodayaYogasvarodaya@Yogasvarodaya but also with Sundardās'sSundardas@Sundardās sarvangayoga 3.25a: lakṣayoga hai sugam upāī |is explained. There are five subdivisions of this Lakṣyayoga: 1. The upper focus (ūrdhvalakṣya)Laksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!urdhvalaksya@ūrdhvalakṣya, 2. The lower focus (adholakṣya)Laksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!adholaksya@adholakṣya, 3. The outer focus (bāhyalakṣya)Laksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!bahyalaksya@bāhyalakṣya, 4. The middle focus (madhyalakṣya)Laksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!madhyalaksya@madhyalakṣya, 5. The inner focus (antaralakṣya)Laksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!antaralaksya@antaralakṣya.In most other texts it is called antarlakṣya, but the TattvayogabinduTattvayogabindu@Tattvayogabindu reads antaralakṣya throughout its manuscript tradition. This is confirmed by the HaṭhasaṅketacandrikāHathasanketacandrika@Haṭhasaṅketacandrikā (cf. sources).The practices of Lakṣ(y)ayoga in Sundardās's sarvangayoga 3.35–36 (Ed. pp. 104–105) are essentially identical, except presented in a different order and subsumed under the category of HaṭhayogaHathayoga@Haṭhayoga. The ssplonavla, one of Rāmacandra'sRamacandra@Rāmacandra central sources, particularly for the second half of his text, describes three almost identical lakṣyas in 2.26–31: antarlakṣya, bahirlakṣya and madhyamaṃ lakṣyaṃ.NārāyaṇatīrthaNarayanatirtha@Nārāyaṇatīrtha, in his yogacandrika, does not mention any of the five categories within his descriptions of Lakṣyayoga. Here, Lakṣyayoga is connected to YogasūtraYogasutra@Yogasūtra 1.35. Lakṣyayoga directs the mind onto a specific focus, like the tip of the nose, etc., to stop the mind's activity, cf. yogacandrika, Ed. p. 54.\flushpage

[14. The upper focus]
[XIV. The upper focus] \phantomsection At first, the upper focusLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!urdhvalaksya@ūrdhvalakṣya is explained. The gaze is on the centre of the sky.Laksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!gaze fixationThis could be the zenith; see petersburger3.And then, having directed the mind upwards, it is fixed [there]. As a result of stabilising this focus, unity of the gaze with the splendour of the highest lord arises. And then, some object that has not been seen before arises in the centre of the sky. That [object] arises in the range of sight of the practitioner. This alone is the upper focus.SundardāsSundardas@Sundardās presents a comparable understanding of ūrdhvalakṣ(y)a, namely the practice of fixing the gaze on the sky, in his sarvangayogaSarvangayoga@Sarvāṅgayoga 3.27: ūrddha lakṣa karai ihīṃ bhāṃtī | duṣṭyākāśa rahai dina rātī | bibidha prakāra hoi ujiyārā | gopi padāratha dīsahiṃ sārā ||A similar practice is presented in bäumer2013 84: ākāśaṃ vimalam paśyan kṛtvā dṛṣṭiṃ nirantarām | stabdhātmā tatkṣaṇād devi bhairavaṃ vapur āpnuyāt || Although the term lakṣya is not used, the central elements of the practice are found here: the gaze is constantly fixed on the sky, establishing a connection with the divine. See also mallinson2007 5.30–31.\flushpage

[15. The lower focus] 1mm
[XV. The lower focus] \phantomsection Now, the lower focusLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!adholaksya@adholakṣya. One should stabilize the gaze up to twelve finger breadths above the nose. Alternatively, one should stabilize the gaze onto the tip of the nose. The gaze becomes still due to the stabilising of the two foci. The breath becomes stable.Laksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!breath stabilization Lifespan increases.In Sundardās'sSundardas@Sundardās sarvangayogaSarvangayoga@Sarvāṅgayoga 2.26 (Ed. p. 104), one finds the following verse with a similar concept. He shares the technique of fixing the gaze onto the nose and the notion of the breath becoming stabilised: prathamahīṃ adho lakṣa kauṃ jānaiṃ | nāśā agra dṛṣṭi sthira ānaiṃ | yātoṃ mana pavanā thira hoī | adho lakṣa jo sādhai koī ||In his hathasamketacandrikachennaiHathasanketacandrika@Haṭhasaṅketacandrikā, SundaradevaSundaradeva adds further techniques to the category of adholakṣya at this point of the text. For the reconstructed passage (based on ORI B220, GOML R3239, and MMPP 2244) and its translation, see p.~.This pair is also taught as an external focus.This statement associates the two practices of adholakṣya with bāhyalakṣya, which is described later in the text. Indeed, these later descriptions instruct the practitioner to focus on one of the five elements at various distances in front of the nose or above the head (cf. p. ).[Then] the focus of emptiness, which is like space, should be executed internally and externally.The description undoubtedly derives from the YogasvarodayaYogasvarodaya@Yogasvarodaya as quoted in the ramatosana (Ed. p. 834), where it is declared a practice of antaralakṣ(y)a. RāmacandraRamacandra@Rāmacandra extracts this passage from his source text and locates this practice within the adholakṣya category.The fear of death does not arise due to meditation on the voidLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!meditation on emptiness in all states while eating, moving, waking [and] at the time of rest.The translation of sthitikāle as ``time of rest'' is confirmed by the four states mentioned in the YSv (cf. sources). The formulation sthitikāle is Rāmacandra's rendering of suṣupteṣu.The concept of five lakṣ(y)as appears only in the lost Yogasvarodaya and from there made its way into ramatosana, yogakarnikaYogakarnika@Yogakarṇikā and TattvayogabinduTattvayogabindu@Tattvayogabindu. Other texts that include it are sarvangayoga, hathasamketacandrikamysore and yogacandrikaYogacandrika@Yogacandrikā. In those texts, it is treated as a distinct type of yoga: Lakṣ(y)yogaLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga. If one encounters the concept of three lakṣ(y)a as found in netratantraNetratantra@Netratantra (cf. 7.1), shivayogapradipikaSivayogapradipika@Śivayogapradīpikā (cf. 4.36–50), mandalabrah (cf. 2.6–2.14) or advaya (Ed. pp. 3–5) etc. it is never presented as a distinct type of yoga.

[16. The physical sign of a person who is engaged in Rājayoga]
[XVI. The physical sign of a person who is engaged in Rājayoga] \phantomsection Now, the physical sign of a person who is engaged in RājayogaRajayoga@RājayogaRajayoga@Rājayoga!physical signs is taught.The shift from LakṣyayogaLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga to the physical sign of Rājayoga seems abrupt, but RāmacandraRamacandra@Rāmacandra follows the YogasvarodayaYogasvarodaya@Yogasvarodaya's structure, treating the remaining Lakṣyayogas later.He is rich at all times.Rajayoga@Rājayoga!wealthIn light of Rāmacandra's understanding of Rājayoga as the ``yoga for kings,'' this translation for pūrṇa seems appropriate.He exists detached from the world [yet] having permeated the world.Cf. sarvangayogaSarvangayoga@Sarvāṅgayoga 3.22: icchā parai tahāṃ so jāī | tīni loka mahiṃ aṭaka na kāī | svarga jāī devani mahiṃ baiṭhai | nāgaloka pātāla su paiṭhai || 22 ||For whom neither birth nor death exists; happiness does not exist; suffering does not exist;Equanimity towards oppositesRajayoga@Rājayoga!equanimity in the state of Rājayoga is common among texts that teach Rājayoga, cf. e.g. amanaskaed 1.26ab: sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ na jānāti śītoṣṇaṃ ca na vindati |; hp 4.111 ≈ nadabindu 53ab−54cd: na vijānāti śītoṣṇaṃ na duḥkhaṃ na sukhaṃ tathā | na mānaṃ nopamānaṃ ca yogī yuktaḥ samādhinā ||; also cf. sarvangayoga 3.18cd: jākaiṃ dukha aru sukha nahiṃ hoī | harṣa śoka vyāpai nahiṃ koī |lineage does not exist; moral conduct does not exist;Cf. datta2024 186.[and] abode does not exist in the mind of this accomplished [person], a light that is connected to God becomes perceptible. And, the light is not cold, not hot, neither white nor yellow.Cf. amanaskaed 1.51: vāsarārdhalayenāpi svātmajyotiḥ prakāśate | sūryo gobhir ivoddīpto yogī viśvaṃ prakāśate |; also cf. sarvangayoga 3.13cd: rājayoga saba ūpara chājai | jo sādhai so adhika birājai ||; and 3.23cd: hṛdai prakāśa rahai dina rātī | deśai jyoti tela bina vātī ||Neither does he have a caste, nor does he have any sign. Furthermore, he is without parts, immaculate and uncharacterised. And then, whatever wish for the most excellent fruit, affectionate woman, etc. arises,This statement is unusual as it contradicts standard renunciatory principles. For this reason, bhavati was changed to na bhavati in the transmission of the \gamma group. The passage is supported by the Yogasvarodaya: \ldots mahājyotir vāñchāṃ bhogaṃ dadāti ca | cf. sources.he obtains that very enjoyment.For constructions similar to ``yasya yasyecchā \ldots taṃ taṃ bhogaṃ \ldots '' cf. anandakanda 1,15.312 and hathatattvakaumudi 5.39.However, his very mind does not experience attachment in this situation.Nearly all manuscripts omit (some even repeat) sentences in this section, likely due to eye skipping caused by structural similarity and brevity of the sentences.

[17. Another sign of Rājayoga]
[XVII. Another sign of Rājayoga] \phantomsection Another sign of RājayogaRajayoga@Rājayoga is described. For whom,Grammatical constructions in this text may deviate from classical Sanskrit. In most cases, however, these should not be regarded as errors due to their frequency but as features of contemporary or regional usage.Sanskrit!regional usage Some constructions in this section and other passages of the text use the genitivegenitive as a substitute for other cases, such as the dative, instrumental or locative; see whitney1879. In particular, this can be observed in this and other places of the text in relative clause constructionsrelative constructions beginning with yasyayasya@yasya, which must, for example, be read as yasminyasmin@yasmin, as otherwise, the corresponding correlative pronoun seems to be missing. The genitive, for example, in connection with the following word manasi or manaḥ (see edition text) would make the yogin the implicit subject of the sentence and the actual correlative pronoun of the construction referring to yasya, in this section ayam or saḥ, would appear incongruous. At the same time, the daṇḍasdanda@daṇḍa in these constructions should be understood as commas or semicolons.even if a kingdom has been attained, there is no gaining of a [karmic] result;Mallinson suggested considering an emendation of phalalābhaḥ to phalalobhaḥ, which would indeed make good sense. However, in light of the unequivocal consistency of the manuscripts across the stemma, I have adhered to the transmitted reading.[and] even in loss, suffering does not arise within the mind; and neither does desire arise. And then, if a certain object has been attained, no aversionThe most common meaning of the word anicchā is indifference. However, even with considerable semantic latitude, this cannot be the intended meaning in this context. For this reason, I propose the meaning of ``aversion'' as attested in petersburger. The meaning ``aversion'' can be easily derived by taking an icchā as a nañ samāsa compound that expresses the direct opposite of ``desire''. The mention of the word tṛṣṇā in the previous sentence supports this conclusion.arises towards [this] certain object, and also no affection of the mind arises towards this very object this is said to be Rājayoga. Moreover, whose mind is impartial towards a person who has expertise in sacred scriptures, a friend [or] an enemy; and [whose] view becomes indifferent; in whose mind no sense of being the agent prevails [while] moving in the whole world and enjoying pleasures; in whose mind the pride of the ability [to do these things] does not arise; [and] who does not present himself as the agent among his attendants this is also said to be Rājayoga.

div.note: 1.5em Whether one is wearing new clothes made of silk, or old, worn [clothes] with holes, whether [one is] smeared with sandalwood and musk, or smeared with mud when delight and grief do not reside within the mind, it is that which is RājayogaRajayoga@Rājayoga.Rajayoga@Rājayoga!equanimity When the mind is neither [in a state of] lack nor [in a state of] abundance, whether one is situated in a city, a forest, an uninhabited village or a village full of people, this too is Rājayoga.
div.div:
[18. Caryāyoga]
[XVIII. Caryāyoga] \phantomsection Now, CaryāyogaCaryayoga@CaryāyogaCaryayoga@Caryāyoga!characteristics is explained.Caryāyoga is absent in the YSv (PT and YK). RāmacandraRamacandra@Rāmacandra uses a passage from the YSv’s section on RājayogaRajayoga@Rājayoga to construct this subtype of yoga (cf. PT, p. 835: nityollāse … samo 'pi ca |). Its brevity suggests an attempt to match the initial list of yogas . The passage does not clarify why he employs the term caryā°. Its inclusion among the fifteen yogas reflects the four pādas of the Śaiva Āgamas (kriyā , jñāna , caryā , and yogapāda). However, there is no connection to ritual conduct/discipline of Śaiva practices. Perhaps, in this context, the concept of caryā° = √car + kṛt suffix yā f. might express the action, which refers to the meaning ``wandering, roaming'' of the verbal root √car, which Rāmacandra brings up in his description.Formless, permanent, immovable [and] unsplittable such is the self.Caryayoga@Caryāyoga!formless self For one whose mind remains steady in such a self, his self does not come into contact with sin and merit. Just as contact with water does not arise for the lotus leaf situated in water, likewise in the [case of the] self. When the mind is absorbed into the formless, in the same way as the wind wanders according to its own will in space, only that is Caryāyoga.Caryayoga@Caryāyoga!wandering in spaceParallels to Rāmacandra's innovative Caryāyoga can be identified in the texts with similar taxonomies. In yogacandrikaYogacandrika@Yogacandrikā (Ed. pp. 2, 52–53, 100–101, 150) NārāyaṇatīrthaNarayanatirtha@Nārāyaṇatīrtha presents Caryāyoga in the context of YogasūtraYogasutra@Yogasūtra 1.33. According to Nārāyaṇatīrtha's commentary, its practice involves the cultivation of specific mental attitudes, such as maitrī (``loving kindness''), karuṇā (``compassion''), muditā (``compassionate joy'') and upekṣā (``equanimity''), towards circumstances characterised by happiness, suffering, virtue and vice. SundardāsSundardas@Sundardās, in his sarvangayogaSarvangayoga@Sarvāṅgayoga (2.40–51, Ed. pp. 96–98), describes the similar sounding Cārcāyoga as a type of bhaktiyoga that is bhakti towards the unmanifest consciousness (avyakta puruṣa) in rapturous devotion. According to Sundardās, the unmanifest consciousness (avyakta puruṣa) is formless, eternal, etc. (40). However, in Sanskrit and brājbhāṣā the term means ``discussion''. Thus Caryāyoga and Carcāyoga are unrelated. For an analysis of Caryāyoga, p.~.

[19. haṭhayogaḥ]

[19. Haṭhayoga]
[XIX. Haṭhayoga] \phantomsection Now, HaṭhayogaHathayoga@HaṭhayogaHathayoga@Haṭhayoga!first type is explained.See p.~ for a detailed discussion of Haṭhayoga within the complex early modern yoga taxonomies.The YogasvarodayaYogasvarodaya@Yogasvarodaya's description of the two types of Haṭhayoga is quoted in shabdakalpadruma (ŚKD), Ed. p. 501. I recorded the variants in the sources of the edition of this passage. I would like to thank Franz Veit for drawing my attention to this reference.Breath is to be controlled by means of practices such as exhalation, inhalation [and] retention, etc.Hathayoga@Haṭhayoga!breath controlThe Yogasvarodaya suggests that the term ādi should refer to the other common practices of Haṭhayoga such as āsana, mudrā, and perhaps even nādānusandhāna, cf. hathapradipika2024 1.56.And then due to the six actions (ṣaṭkarma)Hathayoga@Haṭhayoga!ṣaṭkarma, like dhauti etc.,See hathapradipika2024 2.22–37.the purification of the body arises.Hathayoga@Haṭhayoga!body purification When the breath fills the inside of the sun channel,Usually the sūryanāḍī is the piṅgalā channel, beginning at the right nostril, as previously declared in the TattvayogabinduTattvayogabindu@Tattvayogabindu 3 l. 3. Here, it appears more likely that sūryanaḍī refers to the central channel, the suṣūmnā. However, the manuscript's tradition is clear. Nonetheless, the term might very well be corrupted. The context instead suggests conjecturing the reading śūnyanāḍī. In Jyotsnā 4.10, Brahmānanda understands ``the void'' (śūnya) as the central channel. In Haṭhapradīpikā 3.4, śūnyapadavī is a synonym of suṣumnā. Both words sūrya° and śūnya° begin with a sibilant, which is often confused, followed by a long ū in both manuscripts. Although both words end with orthographically quite distinct ligatures rya 0.2em (rya) or nya 0.2em (nya), an illegible manuscript at an early stage of transmission could easily have caused this error.then the mind is immovable. When the mind is motionless, then the nature of bliss manifests. As a result of Haṭhayoga, the mind becomes absorbed into emptiness. Time [as death] does not approach. \flushpage

[20. Second type of Haṭhayoga]
[XX. Second type of Haṭhayoga] \phantomsection Now, the second typeThe division of HaṭhayogaHathayoga@Haṭhayoga into two subcategories is unique in yoga literature and originates from the YogasvarodayaYogasvarodaya@Yogasvarodaya.of Haṭhayoga is explained.Hathayoga@Haṭhayoga!second typeAt this point Yogasvarodaya as quoted with reference in YogakarṇikāYogakarnika@Yogakarṇikā 12.23, adds a verse not found in the ramatosana: susthāsanaṃ samāsīno nīrajāyatalocanaḥ | cintayet paramātmānaṃ yo vadet sa bhaviṣyati |Some kind of form being white, yellow, blue [and] red, equal to the shine of ten million suns shall be contemplated in one's own bodyHathayoga@Haṭhayoga!light meditation from the feet to the top of the head. As a result of meditation on that, the burning of diseases in the entire body arises. The lifespan increases.Cf. Yogasvarodaya (PT, p. 835) as presented in the sources for 20. p.~: ``Now, listen to the second variation of Haṭhayoga. Contemplate the space at the tip of the nose as being equal to the radiance of ten million suns in colours such as white, red, yellow, black, and other colours of that nature. By meditating in this way, one can achieve a long life because one is freed from the process of ageing (aṅgajaraṇavarjitaḥ em.] aṅgājananavarjitaṃ PT). Through the devoted practice of Haṭhayoga, one whose self is great becomes like Śiva. Having become like the light, one truly becomes one with Śiva inside. Therefore, the path of Haṭhayoga will bring forth supernatural abilities and is followed by the Siddhas.'' RāmacandraRamacandra@Rāmacandra's adaptation omits various details, but both descriptions are reminiscent of Bāhyalakṣya, see section 23 on p.~. Another light based technique of Haṭhayoga, classified as a technique of dhyāna, can be found in liersch2026 33 50. It involves visualising equally intense light at the navel, heart and head, igniting this light in all six cakras, and ultimately attaining liberation from the fetters of birth (mucyante janmabandhanāt). Another similarity appears in amanaskaed 2.7–8: cittaṃ buddhir ahaṅkāra ṛtvijaḥ somapaṃ manaḥ | indriyāṇi daśa prāṇāñ juhoti jyotimaṇḍale || 7 || āmūlād bilaparyantaṃ vibhāti jyotimaṇḍalam | yogibhiḥ satataṃ dhyeyam aṇimādyaṣṭasiddhidam || These verses precede or introduce śāmbhavī mudrā. Here, thought, intellect and ego are taught to be the officiants, whereas the mind is the sacrificer who sacrifices the senses and the ten vital breaths into the orb of light (2.7). The orb of light (jyotimaṇḍala) shines from the root (one immediately thinks of the root of the body or spine, but birch2013 suggests the palate) to the aperture at the top of the head. Yoga practitioners should constantly meditate on it to achieve siddhis (2.8).\flushpage

[21. The characteristics of Jñānayoga]
[XXI. The characteristics of Jñānayoga] \phantomsection Now, the characteristic of JñānayogaJnanayoga@Jñānayoga is explained. 21.1 He shall see the world as only one, illumined by the supreme self. By the method of non dualistic thinking, he may accomplish Jñānayoga. 21.2 Alternatively, wherever one dwells, the world is made of all knowledge. He who knows thus by realisation is also qualified for gnosis. 21.3 The one who is devoted to non dualitynon dualityJnanayoga@Jñānayoga!non duality always attains the reality of ŚaṃbhuSambhu@Śaṃbhu!reality ofJnanayoga@Jñānayoga!reality of Śaṃbhu,RāmacandraRamacandra@Rāmacandra uses the term śāṃbhavīṃ sattāṃsambhavi satta@śāṃbhavī sattā as a designation of the ultimate state to be attained by practising Jñānayoga, which he presents as the realization of absolute unity. In medieval yoga texts, particularly in the RājayogaRajayoga@Rājayoga genre, the feminine noun śāmbhavī most often appears in the context of a non physical mudrā, the so called śāṃbhavī mudrāsambhavi mudra@śāṃbhavī mudrā. For a detailed discussion of śāṃbhavī mudrā, its influence and all references, see birch2013. The usage of the feminine noun śāmbhavī to qualify a state is less common. More frequently one finds the masculine adjective śāṃbhava in order to qualify an exalted yogic state. See for example Candrāvalokana 2, Haṭhapradīpikā 4.7, Anubhavanivedana 1, Haṭhatattvakaumudī 49.27. The idea has its roots in tantric traditions of ŚaivismSaivism@Śaivism and refers to a meditative state associated with ŚivaSiva@Śiva.just as the seed of the banyan tree scattered onto the ground [always] becomes a tree.In rituals the banyan tree (nyagrodha) is associated with the kṣatriya class (smith1998). 21.4 By nature [the reality of ŚaṃbhuSambhu@Śaṃbhu!reality of] is not only seen as one [but] has been fabricated tenfold. [Just as] the branches, buds and twigs are [held] up by the stem of the roots and shoots. [\ldots ]

div.note: 21.5 [\ldots ] The resin, flower [and] fruit are in the seed. This is the extent [of it] by nature. Thus, that [reality] is pure, eternal, unchanging, and immaculate.

21.6 [It] is one, [and] not one, self existing and as a result of its own power it is many things, [as] a modification of five [gross] elements,The term pañcatattvapancatattva@pañcatattva refers to the five gross elements. The concept of five gross elements emerging from a supreme god is found in tantric works, cf. e.g. sivasvarodaya 6–8: nirañjano nirākara eko devo maheśvaraḥ | tasmād ākāśam utpannam ākāśād vāyusambhavaḥ || 6 || vayos tejas tataś cāpas tataḥ pṛthvī samudbhavaḥ | etāni pañcatattvāni vistīrṇāni ca pañcadhā || 7 || tebhyo brahmāṇḍam utpannaṃ tair eva parivartate | vilīyate ca tatraiva tatraiva ramate punaḥ || 8 || ``Faultless and without a body is the one god, the great supreme ruler. From him, the ether element (ākāśa) originated, and from the ether element, the air element came into existence (6). From the air element, the fire element and from the fire element, the water element and from the water element, the earth element. These five elements unfold in a fivefold manner (7). From these five elements, the universe has arisen, evolves and dissolves. [Then] right here, right there [it] enjoys again (8).''thinking mind, intellect, illusion and individuation.In the tantric traditions of Śaivism tenfold tattva systemstattva@tattva!tenfold systems existed from a very early period, see goodall2016. RāmacandraRamacandra@Rāmacandra, as can be seen in the sources of the edition for this passage, is faithful to his source text. However, the exact origin of this specific arrangement of tattvas remains unknown. I discussed the system with Dominic Goodall, who has never encountered it. In Rāmacandra's tenfold systemJnanayoga@Jñānayoga!tenfold tattva system, the one self existing reality must be counted as the first tattva. The term vikriyavikriya@vikriya functions as a placeholder for all further modifications of the one self existing reality. Other tattva systems provide similar concepts such as ahaṃkāravikrīyaahamkaravikriya@ahaṃkāravikrīya (``transformations of ahaṃkāra'') which refers to lesser tattvas like the jñānendrīyas, karmendrīyas and tanmātras.

21.7 Thus, everything is tenfold, extendingThe manuscripts read savistara, which is nonsensical in this context. Thus, I emended according to the source text’s reading.as far as the Lokāloka[ mountain]Lokaloka@Lokāloka mountain.birch2013 suggested that lokāloka be understood as the mythical mountain that divides the visible world from the regions of darkness; see apte1890practical (1980: 933).There is only one. There is nothing else. One who knows this is a knower of truth. \flushpage

div.note: 1.5em The stationary circuit of mundane existencesamsara@saṃsāra!stationary and moving forms consists of the earth, trees, mountains, etc. The moving circuit of mundane existence consists of humans, elephants, horses, birds, etc. Now, that which is the object of sight is called the visible. That which is not seen by sight is called the invisible. In this way, through the vision of unity, the distinction of one's self from the circuit of mundane existence is to be removed. Only this is JñānayogaJnanayoga@Jñānayoga. From the execution of this, time [as death] does not bring about the destruction of the body.RāmacandraRamacandra@Rāmacandra’s prose following XXI.7 picks up the preceding verses’ metaphysical non dualism and apparently elaborates his soteriological exposition of Jñānayoga. By distinguishing between the stationary and moving ``circuits'' of existence (earth, mountains, trees versus humans, animals, etc.) and between the visible and invisible domains, he delineates the full scope of saṃsārasamsara@saṃsāra as a unified field of experience. The yogin’s task is to dissolve the imagined boundary between self and this totality—``through the vision of unity'' (ekadarśana)ekadarsana@ekadarśanaJnanayoga@Jñānayoga!unity of self and saṃsāra—so that perceiver and perceived are no longer opposed. In this realization, all beings and visible and invisible phenomena are apprehended as expressions of one and the same reality, ŚaṃbhuSambhu@Śaṃbhu!reality of. Hence, JñānayogaJnanayoga@Jñānayoga is not merely an intellectual affirmation of oneness but a contemplative practice of erasing dualistic perception. The final statement, that ``time [as death] does not bring about the destruction of the body,'' implies liberation from temporal identification: once unity is realised, kālakala@kāla!as death loses its power to destroy, for the knower no longer identifies with the perishable body but with the timeless selfself!timeless.\flushpage

[22. svabhāvabhedam]

div.head: [22. Distinction of the nature]
div.p: [XXII. Distinction of the nature]
div.note: Now, the nature of the self and its distinctionThe term svabhāvabhedasvabhavabheda@svabhāvabheda appears in philosophical systems to signify the division or distinction of essential natures. For a Buddhist example, see balcerowicz2011dharmakirti. In some Nyāya texts, the term is picked up to refer to different essential properties of the self, see ogawa2023perception. In the NetratantantraNetratantra@Netratantra, the term bhāvabheda occurs frequently in a similar sense as in this passage of the TattvayogabinduTattvayogabindu@Tattvayogabindu. For example cf. Netratantra 16.20–21: bhaviṣyanti mahādevi kaliḥ kaṣṭataro yataḥ | tadarthaṃ paramārtho 'yaṃ mayā te prakaṭīkṛtaḥ | paramārthaḥ paratvena mṛtyujit sarvatomukhaḥ | bhāvabhedena yaṣṭav yo mokṣasiddhim abhīpsatā | Here, however, the context is unphilosophical and specifically intended to signify the phenomenological distinction of the self.is described. Just as the seed of the banyan tree transforms into the shape of the banyan tree [and] thus attains the tenfold distinctionsvabhavabheda@svabhāvabheda!tenfold distinction `root, shoot, bark, branch, twig, bud, the unfolding flower, flower, fruit and resin' by virtue of its nature, in the same way, the pure, unchanging, immaculate one attains such [a distinction] precisely because of the nature of the self [namely], the various forms and modifications of earth, water, fire, wind, space, mind, intellect, illusion, [and individuation.]Rāmacandra's tenfold taxonomy of tattvastattva@tattva!Rāmacandra's tenfold taxonomy may seem inconsistent at first sight. It is probable, however, that ahaṃkāra was lost in the course of the text's transmission given its inclusion in the list of the previous section. Perhaps the discovery of new textual witnesses of the text will solve this problem in the future. None of the tenfold tattva systems known to me correspond exactly to Rāmacandra's system. Taxonomies of tattvas such as kaushik1993 7.4, in which Kṛṣṇa presents a list of eight divisions of prakṛti, are almost identical (bhūmir āpo 'nalo vāyuḥ khaṃ mano buddhir eva cha | ahankāra itīyaṃ me bhinnā prakṛitir aṣhṭadhā ||7.4||). ``Earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego these are the eight divisions of original nature.'' In this list we find most of the elements of Rāmacandra's list, except for the term māyā. The description of kuṇḍalinīKundalini@Kuṇḍalinī in yajnavalkya 4.21 incorporates this system. Another system of ten tattvas appears in Uttarasūtra 1.9–1.13 of nisvasa2015 where the tenfold nature of Sadāśiva is homologised with the mantra. Here the following list is given: prakṛti, puruṣa, niyati, kāla, māyātattva, vidyā, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, dehavyāpin and Śakti, see goodall2016. There is no similarity between the two tenfold tattva systems. However, \ldots As a result of the power of JñānayogaJnanayoga@Jñānayoga, the conviction arises that `the self is only one'self!unity. \flushpage
