div.note: 2.2em since Rājayoga is rooted in ancient ŚaivismSaivism@Śaivism (see birch2019saiva), and Rāmacandra usually tends to present simplified and transsectarian systems, the choice of a tenfold tattva system could be considered a remnant of these ancient systems.\phantomsection 1.5em Just as the single soil in some places appears soft, in some places beautiful, in some places is endowed with fragrance, in some places without fragrance, in some places [the earth is] gold, in some places silver, in some places [it contains] gems,The description of the soil at this point is not clear. The coloured soil mentioned next suggests soil of golden and silver colours and of the colour of precious stones. However, the parallel formulations in the YogasvarodayaYogasvarodaya@Yogasvarodaya (i.e. svarṇarūpā dhāturūpā citrā ratnamayī parā |) instead suggest soil containing the metals or precious stones in question.in some places, appears white, in some places black, in some places red, in some places yellow, in some places appears in variegated colour, in some places like various fruit, in some places like flowers, in some places like a liquid, [and that] only because of its nature. 1.5em In the same way, the self also takes the form of a human, a bird, a deer, an elephant, a Vidyādhara, a Gandharva, a centaur, a great scholar or a great fool, a sick or healthy person, an angry or peaceful person, by virtue of its inherent nature. Through JñānayogaJnanayoga@Jñānayoga, [the self] is known as being free from changes of form. \flushpage

div.note: 1.5em Just as the place of origin of the fruit is only one, but the fruit's destiny is seen as manifold one fruit falls to the ground and dries up; a bee drinks one fruit's juice; a woman places a garland made of one fruit over her voluptuous bosom; one fruit is placed upon a dead person — that is the own nature of the thing. In the same way, the one selfself!unity enjoys eight enjoymentseight enjoyments due to its own nature.RāmacandraRamacandra@Rāmacandra demonstrates that it is perfectly natural for an ātmanatman@ātman!enjoyment to enjoy the eight pleasures. To illustrate this, he uses a random everyday object as an example. With this everyday object, the fruit, different experiences, and actions are naturally produced by different actors, although they all have a single origin the fruit. In the same way, there is only one selfself!unity, as Rāmacandra explained earlier, and it naturally manifests as different beings and experiences different things. The phenomenon Rāmacandra wants to address with this example is that it is natural for the one ātman to enjoy the eight enjoymentseight enjoyments described in the following verse and the prose section on the next page.What are the eight enjoyments?eight enjoymentsThe origin of the aṣṭau bhogāḥeight enjoyments is uncertain. However, the term is mentioned as one of the results of RājayogaRajayoga@Rājayoga!eight enjoyments in the SarvāṅgayogapradīpikāSarvangayogapradipika@Sarvāṅgayogapradīpikā in which SundardāsSundardas@Sundardās takes Rājayoga as that which is commonly known to be vajrolīmudrāvajrolimudra@vajrolīmudrā. Cf. Sarvāṅgayogapradīpikā 3.16: dīsai saṃga pūni muktā | aṣṭa prakāra bhoga kau bhuktā | pāpa puṇya kachu parasai nāṃhīṃ | jaisaiṃ kamala rahai jala māṃhīṃ || 16 || In the MānasollāsaManasollasa@Mānasollāsa of King SomeśvaraSomesvara@Someśvara, one finds the mention of twenty royal upabhogasupabhoga@upabhoga!royal enjoyments, which, however, include all of the eight pleasures in greater detail, cf. manasollasa. This alludes to the possibility of an exceptionally wealthy lifestyleRajayoga@Rājayoga!wealth and sensual pleasures for Rāmacandra's audienceTattvayogabindu@Tattvayogabindu!intended audience mentioned in section 1.

22.1 A good perfume, fine clothing, a good bed, a beautiful woman and a good charioteer,Several plausible readings exist for the fifth element among the eight pleasures. The reading sudeham, as an outlier, is probably a later correction. Moreover, although susthānam (``a good site'') would be a simple and plausible solution, the stemma suggests the reading susthātā (``a good charioteer''). This word has only survived in an incorrect grammatical form and needs to be corrected. This choice is supported, among other things, by the fact that a total of eight pleasures must be mentioned in this verse, which is only possible if the last word of the fourth pāda is read as sudhiṣaṇam (``a good dwelling place''), which makes the reading susthānam redundant. Additionally, Rāmacandra himself introduces a horse as one of the eight enjoyments in the following paragraph of the TattvayogabinduTattvayogabindu@Tattvayogabindu. Thus, susthātā as an element related to vehicles is plausible.food, drink, [and a] good dwelling place. Those are the eight enjoyments. \flushpage

div.note: 1.5em The comparison with the corresponding passage in the source text reveals once again Rāmacandra'sRamacandra@Rāmacandra positive and anti ascetic attitudeRajayoga@Rājayoga!anti ascetic orientation towards wealth and sensual pleasuresRajayoga@Rājayoga!wealth and sensual pleasures in his Rājayoga.1. Clothes made from silk thread;Within the twenty upabhogas of the MānasollāsaManasollasa@Mānasollāsa there is the topic of Vastropabhogaupabhoga@upabhoga!Vastropabhoga@Vastropabhoga (``enjoyment of garments''). Particularly in summer, the king is asked to wear silk or cotton clothes which are thin and charming; cf. manasollasa.2. Mansions endowed with five or seven rooms.The first adhyāya of the third viṃśati of the Mānasollāsa discusses astrology for finding out auspicious moments while building new houses for princes. The section describes houses with one to four śālās; cf. manasollasa.3. A very large bed with a soft and lovely blanket;This corresponds to the Śayyābhogaupabhoga@upabhoga!Sayyabhoga@Śayyābhoga within the Mānasollāsa. The section describes seven kinds of beds and eight kinds of bed steads; cf. manasollasa.4. [on which] there is seated a wife belonging to the Padminī classPadmini@Padminī!class of womenCf. ratirahasya, Ed.~p.~6.of women youthful, beautiful and virtuous;This corresponds toyoṣidupabhogaupabhoga@upabhoga!yosidupabhoga@yoṣidupabhoga (``enjoyment of young women'') within the Mānasollāsa. In this chapter, King SomeśvaraSomesvara@Someśvara describes the qualifications of women a king should marry. The two most important qualities he gives are beauty and full youth. Out of the four kinds of women: (a) PadminīPadmini@Padminī, (b) CitriṇīCitrini@Citriṇī, (c) ŚaṅkhinīSankhini@Śaṅkhinī, and (d) HastinīHastini@Hastinī, he suggests that the latter two kinds are not worth enjoying; cf. manasollasa.\phantomsection 5. An excellent seat;The āsanopabhogaupabhoga@upabhoga!asanopabhoga@āsanopabhoga (``the enjoyment of seats'') within the Mānasollāsa describes various kinds of royal seats; cf. manasollasa.6. An exceptionally valuable horse;This corresponds to yānopabhogaupabhoga@upabhoga!yanopabhoga@yānopabhoga (``enjoyment of vehicles'') within the Mānasollāsa. In this section, King Someśvara lists nine kinds of vehicles, including horses; cf. manasollasa.7. Appetising food;This corresponds to annabhogaupabhoga@upabhoga!annabhoga@annabhoga (``enjoyment of food'') within the Mānasollāsa. In this section, King Someśvara describes the names of various kinds of delicious food and the instructions for preparing various dishes; cf. manasollasa.8. Similarly [tasty] drinks.The pānīyabhogaupabhoga@upabhoga!paniyabhoga@pānīyabhoga (``enjoyment of drinks'') section of the Mānasollāsa concerns beverages and their consumption; cf. manasollasa.The eight enjoymentseight enjoyments have been described. They impart suffering. And [they] require begging.To the genre connoisseur, the sentence ``bhīkṣāṃ yācante ca |'' initially seems \ldots \flushpage

[XXIII. bāhyalakṣyam] \phantomsection tocsectionXXIII. bāhyalakṣyam \phantomsection
cf. YSv (PT. p. 837): idānīṃ bāhyalakṣāṇi siddhidāni śṛṇu priye | dhāraṇākhyā tu caitāni jñātavyāni viśeṣataḥ | līlayā bhāvayel līnaṃ jyotiḥpūrṇaṃ mahāparam |cf. SSP 2.28 (Ed. p. 39): atha bahirlakṣyaṃ kathyate | nāsāgrād bahiraṅgulacatuṣṭaye nīlajyotiḥsaṃkāśaṃ lakṣayet |idānīṃ bāhyalakṣyaṃbāhyalakṣaṇabāhyalakṣaṃbāhyalakṣyaḥlakṣaṇaṃlakṣyaṃbāhyalakṣa kathyate/ nāsāgrād ārabhyāṅgulacatuṣṭaya catuṣṭayaṃpramāṇaṃ nīlākāraṃnirākāraṃnilākaraṃ tejaḥteja°jaḥ°pū:rṇam āpūrṇakāmkāśaākāśaṃlakṣyaṃlakṣaṇaṃlakṣaṃ kartavyam/

2.2em suspiciously strange and suggests a corruption of the text. However, the passage is well preserved in the \beta 0.15em and \gamma group. The subject of the sentence is undoubtedly the aṣṭau bhogāḥeight enjoyments. Nevertheless, this statement is aimed at the practitioner. If one takes the transmission of the manuscripts seriously, the question arises as to who would beg for the eight pleasures specified above. A travelling ascetic or mendicantasceticism!mendicancy would ask for food and drink, but certainly not for silk clothes, women, expensive horses, etc. The average householder may aspire to this, but the phrase yācante still seems inappropriate and overshoots the mark. Above all, there is no logical answer as to who exactly would be begged for such valuable objects and women. This statement can, therefore, only be aimed at members of the royal courtTattvayogabindu@Tattvayogabindu!intended audience. The only one able to grant such costly requests can be someone extremely rich or a king himself. This observation perfectly suits the initial definition of RājayogaRajayoga@Rājayoga!definition (cf. 1. ll. 1–2, p. ) in which it is defined as a practice that works even if the practitioner is leading an exuberant wealthy lifestyleRajayoga@Rājayoga!wealth and sensual pleasures. 1.5em Just like the rays of the sun, the ghee of milk, the burning of fire, the stupor from poison, the sesame oil from the sesame seed, the shade from the tree, the sweet odour from a fruit, the fire from a wood log, the sweet taste of sugary things, the cold from piles of snow, etc., is the nature of the thingsvabhava@svabhāva. In the same way, the circuit of mundane existencesamsara@saṃsāra!relation to Paramesvara@relation to Parameśvara is within the highest God's natureParamesvara@Parameśvara!relation to samsara@relation to saṃsāra. Moreover, the highest GodParamesvara@Parameśvara!indivisibility and completeness is indivisible and complete. \phantomsection
[23. The outer focus]
[XXIII. The outer focus] \phantomsection Now, the outer focusBahyalaksya@BāhyalakṣyaLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!bahyalaksya@bāhyalakṣya is taught. Beginning at four finger breadths from the tip of the noseBahyalaksya@Bāhyalakṣya!distance from the nose, the space elementBahyalaksya@Bāhyalakṣya!space elementtattva@tattva!space element, appearing blue and being full of splendour, shall be made into the focus. \flushpage

SSP 2.28 (Ed. p. 39) athavā nāsāgrād ṣaḍaṅgulam adhovāyutattvaṃ dhūmravarṇaṃ lakṣayet | athavā aṣṭāṅgula āraktaṃ tejas tattvaṃ lakṣayet | athavā daśāṅgule kallolavad āpas tattvaṃ lakṣayet | athavā ākāśamukhaṃ dṛṣṭvā lakṣayat kiraṇākulitaṃ paśyati | evaṃ nirmalīkaraṇam | athavordhvadṛṣṭayāntarālaṃ lakṣayet | jyotir mukhāni paśyati | athavā yatra tatrākāśaṃ lakṣayet | ākāśasadṛśaṃ cittaṃ muktipradaṃ bhavati | \approx hathasamketacandrikajodhpur (MMPP 2244, f. 125r ll. 6–7): atha bāhyalakṣyaṃ nirūpyate nāsāgrādārabhyāṃgulacatuṣṭaya 4 pramāṇaṃ pavanatattvaṃ dhūmrākāraṃ lakṣyaṃ karttavyaṃ | athavā nāsāgrād ārabhyāṃguṣṭhāṃgulapramāṇam atiraktaṃ tatvaṃ lakṣyaṃ kartavyaṃ | 2mmathavā nāsāgrād ārabhyanāsāgrārabhyanāsāgrād ābhyaom. ṣaḍaṅguladvadaśaṃgula°om.ṣaḍaṃgulaṃpramāṇaṃ pavanatattvaṃom.+++++ dhūmrākāraṃ+++++ lakṣyaṃlakṣaṇaṃlakṣaṃom. karttavyamom./ athavāathaom. nāsāgrād ārabhyāṣṭāṅgulaārabhyaṃ ṣṭāṃgula°ārabhyā ṣaḍaṃgula°ārabhya ṣaḍaṃgula°ārabhya aṣṭāgula°ārabhya ṣṭāṃgula°om.ārabhyaṃ ṣṭagula°pramāṇam atiraktaṃatirattaṃitiriktaṃom.matiraktaṃ tejoom.teja°lakṣyaṃlakṣaṇaṃlakṣaṃom. karttavyamom./ athavā nāsāgrād ārabhya daśāṅgulapramāṇaṃ śuklaṃom. cañcalam ucaṃdrākāramom.dakaṃom. lakṣyaṃlakṣaṇaṃlakṣyaom.lakṣaṃ kartavyamom./ athavā nāsāgrād ārabhya dvādaśā:ṅgulapramāṇaṃdvādaśā aṃgulapramāṇaṃtattvaṃ dvādaśāṃgulapramāṇaṃ pītavarṇaṃ pṛthvītattvaṃ lakṣyaṃlakṣaṇaṃlakṣaṃ kartavyam/ athavā nāsāgrād ārabhya koṭisūrya:samaprabhaṃ°prabhāṃ tejaḥpūrṇam āpūrṇatejaḥ | pūrṇaṃkāśaakāśa°tattvaṃ lakṣyaṃlakṣaṇaṃlakṣaṃ kartavyam/ ākāśamadhyeom. ākāśopariākāśoparī vāom. dṛṣṭiṃom.dṛṣṭi kṛtvāākāśamadhyekṛtvā ākāśamadhye dhyānakāraṇāt sūryaṃsūrya vinā sūryasaṃbandhinīṃsūryasaṃbadhinīsūryasaṃbaṃdhīnīṃsūryasambandhinī sahasrakiraṇāvalīṃsahasrāṇapi kiraṇāṇisahasrāṇy api kīraṇāṇisahasrakiraṇāvaliṃsahasrakiraṇapaṅktīḥsahasrakiraṇāvali paśyatipaśyatepaśyatīpaśyaṃtipati/

div.note: 1.5em Or, beginning at six finger breadths from the tip of the nose, the wind elementBahyalaksya@Bāhyalakṣya!wind elementtattva@tattva!wind element, in the shape of smoke, shall be made into the focus. 1.5em Or, beginning at eight finger breadths from the tip of the nose, the very red fire elementBahyalaksya@Bāhyalakṣya!fire elementtattva@tattva!fire element shall be made into the focus. 1.5em Or, beginning at ten finger breadths from the tip of the nose, the white fickle water elementBahyalaksya@Bāhyalakṣya!water elementtattva@tattva!water element shall be made into the focus. 1.5em Or, beginning at twelve finger breadths from the tip of the nose, the yellow coloured earth elementBahyalaksya@Bāhyalakṣya!earth elementtattva@tattva!earth element shall be made into the focus.The first five outer fociBahyalaksya@Bāhyalakṣya!five elemental foci, associated with the five elementstattva@tattva!five elements can also be identified in sarvangayogaSarvangayoga@Sarvāṅgayoga 3.29–32: bāhya lakṣa aura puni jāṃnahuṃ | paṃca tatva kī lakṣa su ṭhānahuṃ | agra nāsikā aṃgula cārī | nīla varṇa nabha deṣi bicārī || 29 || nāsā agra aṃgula chaha deṣaiṃ | dhūmrahi varṇa vāyu tata peṣai | aṃgula aṣṭa nāsikā āgai | rakta varṇa su vahni tata jāgai || 30 || nāsā agra aṃgula daśa tāṃīṃ | śveta varṇa jala deṣi tahāṃīṃ | nāsā agra su aṃgula bārā | pīta varṇa bhū deṣi apārā || 31 || bāhya lakṣa aura bahuterī | so jānaiṃ jo pāvai serī | sataguru kṛpā karai jau kabahī | dei batāi chinaka maiṃ sabahī || 32 || ``(29) Contemplate the external focus repeatedly, focusing on the five elements. Four fingers above the tip of the nose contemplate the blue coloured space element. (30) Six fingers from the tip of the nose one visualises the smoke coloured air element. Eight fingers in front of the nose one visualises the red coloured fire element. (31) Ten fingers from the tip of the nose one visualises the white coloured water element. Twelve fingers in front of the nose one visualises the earth element with a yellow colour. (32) Many external foci exist, but only a few can attain the ultimate goal. If the true guruguru@guru!role in Bāhyalakṣya shows mercy, everything is revealed within an instant.''1.5em Or, beginning at the tip of the nose, the space elementBahyalaksya@Bāhyalakṣya!luminous space element full of fire shining like ten million suns shall be made the focus. After having fixed the gazeBahyalaksya@Bāhyalakṣya!gaze fixation on the space element or above the space element, as a result of meditationBahyalaksya@Bāhyalakṣya!meditation, he sees the row of thousand rays connected to the sun without the sun. \flushpage

div.note: Laksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!bahyalaksya@bāhyalakṣya 1.5em Or, the mass of light situated a distance of seventeen finger widths above the head shall be made the focus. Or, at the front of the gaze, the earth element appearing in the colour of molten gold shall be made the focus.A variant of the practice with minor differences can also be found in advaya 6 (Ed. p. 4): atha bahirlakṣyalakṣaṇam | nāsikāgre caturbhiḥ ṣaḍbhir aṣṭabhiḥ daśabhiḥ dvādaśabhiḥ kramāt aṅgulānte nīladyutiśyāmatvasadṛgraktabhaṅgīsphuratpītavarṇadvayopetaṃ vyoma yadi paśyati sa tu yogī bhavati | caladṛṣṭyā vyomabhāgavīkṣituḥ puruṣasya dṛṣṭyagre jyotirmayūkhā vartante | taddarśanena yogī bhavati | taptakāñcanasaṃkāśajyotir mayūkhā apāṅgānte bhūmau vā paśyati taddṛṣṭiḥ sthirā bhavati | śīrṣopari dvādaśāṅgulasamīkṣituḥ amṛtatvaṃ bhavati | yatra kutra sthitasya śirasi vyomajyotir dṛṣṭaṃ cet sa tu yogī bhavati || 6 || ``Now, the characteristics of the outer focus. If one sees a space endowed with two colours, a twinkling yellow breaking into a red which resembles the blackness of profound azure radiance, at [a distance of] four, six, eight, ten and twelve finger breadths, in that order, from the tip of the nose, he becomes a yogin. With the fluctuating gaze of one who looks at the portions of space, luminous rays manifest in front of the observer's field of vision. By seeing that, one becomes a yogin. [Once] he sees luminous rays appearing like molten gold at the corner of his eye or on the ground, his gaze becomes stable. For one who sees [this phenomenon] twelve finger breadths above the head, the state of immortality ensues. If the light of space is seen in the head by one who is situated anywhere, he is a yogin.''Cf. shivayogapradipika 4.41cd–47ab for another description of Bāhyalakṣya closely resembling the one in advaya.The hathasamketacandrikamysore (manuscripts checked: ORI B220, GOML R3239, MMPP 2244) quotes the Bāhyalakṣya passage from the Tattvayogabindu without reference. Yet, Sundaradeva's text appears to be corrupt. Moreover, he selected only some of the techniques presented here; see sources on pp.~–.1.5em As a result of focusing on any one of the discussed foci, wrinkles, grey hair, etc., become remote. Diseases of the limbs become distant without medical herbs. All enemies become friends even while sleeping.It is not entirely clear how svapne 'pi is meant here. Either it is supposed to emphasise the effortlessness of getting rid of all enemies, as this happens ``overnight''. Alternatively, it could also be translated as ``even in a dream'', in the sense that one has got rid of all enemies even in the rather uncontrollable state of dreaming.The lifespan increases up to 1000 years. He recites unlearned scripture with the tip of the tongue. Such are the manifold results. \flushpage

div.head: [24. The inner focus]
div.p: [XXIV. Antaralakṣya]
div.note: Now, the inner focusLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!antaralaksya@antaralakṣya is explained. At the location of the root bulb (mūlakandakanda@kanda)Various concepts of the location of the kanda are found in yogic literature. In the yajnavalkya 4.16–27 one reads: kandasthānāṃ manuṣyāṇāṃ dehamadhyān navāṅgulam | caturaṅgulam utsedham āyāmaś ca tathāvidhaḥ || 16 || aṇḍākṛtivad ākāraṃ bhūṣitaṃ tattvagādhibhiḥ | catuṣpadāṃ tiraścāṃ ca dvijānāṃ tundamadhyame || 17 || ``The location of the bulb (kanda) of humans is nine finger widths from the waist. [It is] four finger widths in height and has the same [measure in] length. It appears like an egg, and [it is] ornamented with the five elements of creation and sustenance. In quadrupeds, birds and other beings, it is in the centre of the belly.'' hathapradipika2024 3.64cd (gulphadeśasamīpe ca kandaṃ tatra prapīḍayet) instructs the yogin to press the kanda with the feet in the context of uḍḍiyāṇabandha, which could imply that the kanda is in the genital region (unless one assumes the very complex and challenging posture termed kandapīḍāsana, cf. encyclopediaasana, pp. 143–144). Sundaradeva, in yuktabhavadeva 7.224 and Bhavadevamiśra in hathasamketacandrikajodhpur (MMPP 2244, f. 36r) argue that the kanda is near the navel. In yogacudamani 14cd the kanda is between the penis and the navel (ūrdhvaṃ meḍhrādadho nābheḥ kande yoniḥ khagāṇḍavat).there is a single white Brahman channel,The term brahmanāḍī is a synonym for the suṣumnā, cf., e.g.~hathapradipika2024~2.46~and~2.67, Gorakṣaśatakamallinson2012sataka 47, yogakundalinyopanisad 37c–38b, yogacintamani (Ed. pp. 46, 112, 116, 140, 191), hatharatnavali 2.8, 2.25, 2.65, 2.69.originating from the staff of BrahmanThe term brahmadaṇḍabrahmadanda@brahmadaṇḍa in this context refers to the spinal column, which is usually identified with Mt. Meru in tantric texts, cf. stupa.and extending up to the aperture of Brahman. The Brahman channel, being within [the staff of Brahman],Naturally, one would read brahmanāḍīmadhye compounded, but this would leave the sentence lacking a subject. Therefore, the only option is to read brahmanāḍī madhye separately, referring to the inside of the previously mentioned brahmadaṇḍa. Assuming another channel within the brahmanāḍībrahmanadi@brahmanāḍī like the citrānāḍīcitranadi@citrānāḍī in mallinson2007 5.160 would be difficult to prove.having the shape of a stalk of a lotus flower [and] shining like ten million suns goes upwards. One such manifestation exists. As a result of meditation on this manifestationCf. bäumer2013 35.the accomplishment of the eight supernatural powerssiddhi@siddhi beginning with `becoming as small as the smallest particle of matter' etc.For a detailed discussion of the yogic siddhis, see yogapowers2017.exists in proximity of the person.Three of the five witnesses of the \gamma group add an incomplete list of the eight siddhis \ldots

div.p: cf. YSv (PT, p. 838): lalāṭopari vā dhyātvā candraṃ vā jyotir īśvaram | nāśayet kuṣṭharogādīn mahāyuṣmān śivaḥ paraḥ | bhruvor madhye 'thavā dhyātvā arkantu teja īśvaram | sthiradṛṣṭau rājapūjyo jīvanmuktaḥ śivo yathā | ātmānam ātmarūpaṃ hi dhyātvā yo niṣkriyo bhavet | nirāśīryatatattvo 'yaṃ itaro na nṛpasthitiḥ |cf. SSP 2.27 (Ed. p. 38): athavā lalāṭordhve gollāṭamaṇḍape sphurattārākāraṃ lakṣayet | \approx hathasamketacandrikajodhpur (MMPP 2244, f. 125v ll. 1–3): athāvā lalāṭopari ākāśamadhye śukladṛśyasya tejaso dhyānakaraṇāc charīrāḥ kuṣṭḥādiroga naśyaṃtīti | athavā bhruvor madhye atiraktavarṇasyātisthūlasya tejaso dhyānakaraṇāt kalānāṃ pārthivapuruṣāṇāṃ vallabho bhavati | taṃ puruṣaṃ dṛṣṭvā sarveṣāṃ puruṣāṇāṃ dṛṣṭiḥ sthirā bhavatī |athavā lalāṭopary āom.lalāṭoparilalāṭoparīkāśamadhyeom. śuklasadṛśasyaom. tejasoom.tejo dhyānakāraṇāc chadhyānakāraṇātom.rīraśarīra°om.sambandhi:naḥ°saṃbaṃdhi°sambandhī kuṣṭhādayokuṣṭādayo rogārogāḥ naśyantinaśyaṃtī/ āyur vṛddhir bhavṛddivatibhavati || cha ||bhavatī/ athavāom. bhruvor mabṛvordhye'tiraktaatirakta°tirikta°varṇasyā:tisthūlasyavarṇasyātī sthalasya'tisthūlasyaḥ tejasotejāso dhyānakaraṇāt sadhyānakāraṇāddhyānaṃ karaṇātkalānāṃsakālānāṃsakalānābahulānāṃ pārthivapuruṣāṇāṃ\phantomsection parthivānāṃ tatpuruṣāṇāṃ ca vallabho bhavatibhavati | jagad vallabho pi bhavati/ taṃasya puruṣaṃ dṛṣṭvāpuruṣaṃ dṛṣṭāpuruṣaṃpuruṣasyāvalokanenapuruṣa° sarveṣāṃpratisarveṣāṃ dṛṣṭiḥ sthirādṛṣṭisthirā bhavatibhavati || cha ||bhavatī//

div.note: 2.2em(see apparatus). I did not include it in greyscale for two reasons. First, the passage is incomplete and in a very corrupt state. Second, since it is absent U2 it probably does not belong to the \gamma group archetype. The passage dure vā yadi vādure śrutvā seems to refer to the supernatural abilities dūradarśana and dūraśravana. The list does not follow the standard list of eight supernatural powers. After the first four items that are usually considered as primary siddhis, the three manuscripts instead list three of the so called secondary siddhis, cf. bhagavata 11.10 and 11.15.2–6. Because of that, it is impossible to determine the missing siddhi precisely. However, the passage allows to identify seven siddhis: Aṇimā (``the ability to reduce size to the size of the smallest particle''), Mahimā (``the ability to expand one's body to an infinitely large size''), Laghimā (``the ability to become weightless or lighter than air''), Garimā (``the ability to become heavy or dense''), Dūraśravaṇa (``hearing things far away''), Dūradarśana (``seeing things far away'') and Parakāyapraveśitā (``entering the bodies of others''). 1.5em Or, as a result of meditation onto the bright light within the space above the forehead, diseases related to the body, skin disease[s], etc., vanish.The ssplonavla 2.27 (Ed. p. 38) includes three techniques of antarlakṣya which are unparalleled in Rāmacandra's system: athavā bhramaraguhāmadhye āraktabhramarākāraṃ lakṣayet | athavā karṇadvayaṃ tarjanībhyāṃ nirodhayet tataḥ śiromadhye dhūṃdhūṃkāraṃ nādaṃ śṛṇoti | athavā cakṣurmadhye nīlajyotirūpaṃ putalyākāraṃ lakṣayed | ``Or, one should focus the form of a very red bee within the bhrahmaraguhā. Or, one should close both ears with the index fingers and listen to the dhūṃ dhūṃ sound in the head. Or, one should focus on the form of a doll appearing in blue light within the eyes.''shivayogapradipika 4.32–41 describes the main practice of antarlakṣya in very similar ways along with two alternatives in 4.40–41 which resemble those in the ssplonavla 2.27: athavā karṇayor dvāre tarjanībhyāṃ nirodhayet | śrīhaṭṭamastake nādaṃ ghuṃghuṃkāraṃ śṛṇoti ca || 40 || cakṣurmadhye 'thavā nīlajyotirūpaṃ vilokayet | antarlakṣyam iti jñeyaṃ bahirlakṣyam atha śṛṇu || 41 || ``(40) Alternatively, one should block the opening of the ears with the index fingers. At the crown of the head, at the śrīhaṭṭa, one hears the sound which makes `ghuṃ ghuṃ'. (41) Likewise, one should visualize the form of blue light within the eyes. Thus, it is known as the internal focus. Now listen to the external fixation.''The lifespan increases. Alternatively, as a result of meditation on the very subtle red light in the middle of the eyebrows, he becomes one who is beloved among all royal people.For the translation of pārthivapuruṣāṇāṃ cf. the usage of pārthiva° in section 1, l. 5.After having seen this person, everybody's gaze becomes fixed [onto him].The placement of the ten channels and vital winds after antaralakṣya rather than madhyalakṣya in both Rāmacandra's Tattvayogabindu and the Yogasvarodaya is puzzling.\flushpage

div.head: [25. Division of the channels]
div.p: [XXV. Division of the channels]
div.note: Now, the divisions of channels within the body are explained. There are ten primary channels.nadi@nāḍīThe notion of ten primary channels can already be found in early texts of Haṭhayoga, cf., e.g., the vivekamartandaolda 17 (Central Library, Baroda Acc. No. 4110, 1534 Saṃvat): teṣu nāḍīsahasreṣu dvisaptatir udāhṛtāḥ | pradhānāḥ prāṇavāhinyo bhūyas tatra daśa smṛtāḥ || ``Of those thousand channels, seventy two have been spoken of, and among them, ten are considered most important. They are the main pathways of the vital breaths.'' Also cf. fausta1976 34. However, the enumeration of ten main channels in yogic literature also has predecessors, e.g., in Śaivasiddhānta, cf. sardha 10.4–5. Other systems, e.g., yajnavalkya 4.26 or vasisthasamhita 2.21, enumerate fourteen primary channels.Among them is a pair of channels. [Their] designation is Iḍānadi@nāḍī!Ida@Iḍā and Piṅgalānadi@nāḍī!Pingala@Piṅgalā [and they] exist at the entrance of the nose. The Suṣumṇānadi@nāḍī!Susumna@Suṣumṇā flows by the path of the palate to the door of Brahman.According to tantrika3 (p. 93), the palate is the Śaiva locus of the central granthi along the course of the breath through five granthis (heart, throat, palate, eyebrows, nose tip), cf. tantraloka 5.111. YSv (PT) alternatively reads bhānumargeṇa ``by the path of the sun.'' In several yogic systems, the microcosmic sun is located at the base of the central channel (see asiddhi 4.1) and ascends upward (see asiddhi 4.11).The brahmadvāra, synonymous with brahmarandhra ``aperture of Brahman,'' denotes the fontanelle through which the yogi’s vital principle exits at death, see rootsofyoga2017.The Sarasvatī[ channel]nadi@nāḍī!Sarasvati@Sarasvatī exists within the mouth. The two channels, Gāndhārīnadi@nāḍī!Gandhari@Gāndhārī and Hastijihvānadi@nāḍī!Hastijihva@Hastijihvā, exist within the two ears. The two channels, Pūṣānadi@nāḍī!Pusa@Pūṣā and Ālaṃbuṣānadi@nāḍī!Alambusa@Ālaṃbuṣā, are situated at the centre of the two eyes. Śaṅkhinīnadi@nāḍī!Sankhini@Śaṅkhinī stretches from the beginning of the opening of the penis through the Iḍā channelnadi@nāḍī!Ida@Iḍā up to the place of Brahman.The brahmasthāna, synonymous with brahmarandhra, is here identified with the sahasrāracakra, cf. dhyanabind 65.Kuhūnadi@nāḍī!Kuhu@KuhūThe list would be incomplete without kuhūnadi@nāḍī!Kuhu@Kuhū, attested only in U2, where it and śaṅkhinīnadi@nāḍī!Sankhini@Śaṅkhinī are swapped. Neither occurs in YSv (PT), but both and their usual locations appear in SSP 1.66, hence my conjecture. I kept the sentence in greyscale as the omission may be authorial.stretches from the entrance of the rootThe root entrance (mūladvāra) here denotes the anus, cf. ssplonavla 1.66: kuhūr gudadvāre vahati ``Kuhū conducts through the anus.''through the Piṅgalā channelnadi@nāḍī!Pingala@Piṅgalā up to the place of Brahman. Such channels are situated at the ten openings. The other channels, numbering 72,000, occur in a subtle form at the roots of the hairs.

div.head: [26. The vital winds within the body]
div.p: [XXVI. The vital winds within the body]
div.note: Now, ten vital winds are situated within the body.vayu@vāyu Their functions are explained. The Prāṇa vital windvayu@vāyu!prana@prāṇa is located within the chest and performs inhalation and exhalation. It brings about the desire for food and drink. Within the anus, the Apāna vital windvayu@vāyu!apana@apāna is situated. It performs contraction [and] restraining. Within the navel, the Samāna vital windvayu@vāyu!samana@samāna exists. It induces the absorption of [substances from]The verbal form śoṣayati (causative third person singular indicative present of √śuṣ) means ``causes to dry up'' or ``causes to disappear''. In this context, however, a better idiomatic translation would be ``causes to absorb'', since the Samāna vital wind absorbs the eaten substances in the body and distributes it everywhere, cf. yajnavalkya 4.55–57 (Ed. p. 40) and 4.69ab (Ed. p. 42).all the channels. In this way, it causes the channels to be nourished, causes appetite to be generated, and causes the [digestive] fire to be kindled. Within the palate, the Udāna vital windvayu@vāyu!udana@udāna is situated. This wind swallows food, [and] it drinks liquid. The Vyāna vital windvayu@vāyu!vyana@vyāna exists in the entire body.I have conjectured nāgavāyuvayu@vāyu!naga@nāga to vyānavāyuvayu@vāyu!vyana@vyāna based on the description provided in YSv (PT), as the latter term generally corresponds to the provided function of this vital wind. From a text critical perspective, however, this choice is difficult and not unambiguous, since according to SSP 1.67 (nāgavāyuḥ sarvāṅgavyāpakaḥ mocakaś cālakaś ca), not just Vyāna (as in YSv) but also Nāgavayu@vāyu!naga@nāga pervades the whole body, a concept also attested in vasisthasamhita 2.49cd and 2.52cd. YSv (PT, pp. 838–839) ascribes the function of belching (udgāra) to Nāgavayu@vāyu!naga@nāga (udgāre nāga ākhyātaḥ ūrdhvavāyuḥ pracālane |) which supports my conjecture. However, Rāmacandra follows SSP 1.67 (Ed. pp. 23–24) by ascribing the function of belching to Kṛkalavayu@vāyu!krkala@kṛkala, even though Ysv ascribes sneezing (kṣut) to Kṛkalavayu@vāyu!krkala@kṛkala. This indicates that he mixed the descriptions of the YSv and SSP, which makes it possible that he followed the SSP in the case of Nāgavayu@vāyu!naga@nāga, too. This leaves us with the other possibility that Vyānavayu@vāyu!vyana@vyāna and its description dropped out. However, in the YSv (PT, pp. 838–839), the order of the ten vital winds is as follows: Prāṇavayu@vāyu!prana@prāṇa, Apānavayu@vāyu!apana@apāna, Samānavayu@vāyu!samana@samāna, Udānavayu@vāyu!udana@udāna, Vyānavayu@vāyu!vyana@vyāna, Kūrmavayu@vāyu!kurma@kūrma, Nāgavayu@vāyu!naga@nāga, Kṛkaravayu@vāyu!krkara@kṛkara, Devadattavayu@vāyu!devadatta@devadatta, Dhanañjayavayu@vāyu!dhananjaya@dhanañjaya. In the SSP 1.67 (Ed. pp. 23–24): Prāṇavayu@vāyu!prana@prāṇa, Apānavayu@vāyu!apana@apāna, Samānavayu@vāyu!samana@samāna, Vyānavayu@vāyu!vyana@vyāna, Udānavayu@vāyu!udana@udāna, Nāgavayu@vāyu!naga@nāga, Kūrmavayu@vāyu!kurma@kūrma, Kṛkaravayu@vāyu!krkara@kṛkara, Devadattavayu@vāyu!devadatta@devadatta, Dhanañjayavayu@vāyu!dhananjaya@dhanañjaya. In both sources, the Vyāna vital windvayu@vāyu!vyana@vyāna appears to be within the group of the first five major vital winds. This group of five winds is undoubtedly common across yogic literature, see rootsofyoga2017. The emergence of Nāgavayu@vāyu!naga@nāga instead of Vyānavayu@vāyu!vyana@vyāna in all the witnesses \ldots Through that vital wind, the body is set in motion. When it is defective, it leads to pain. The Kūrma vital windvayu@vāyu!kurma@kūrma exists within the eyes. \flushpage

div.p: cf. div.note: It performs [the] opening and closing [of the eyes]. Belching arises from the Kṛkala vital windvayu@vāyu!krkala@kṛkala. Yawning arises from the Devadatta vital windvayu@vāyu!devadatta@devadatta. Sound arises from the Dhanañjaya vital windvayu@vāyu!dhananjaya@dhanañjaya.

div.head: [27. Central focus]
div.p: [XXVII. Central focus]
div.note: 2.2emindicates a corruption of the transmission or a mistake by Rāmacandra. The description of the function of the vital wind in this passage makes it slightly more likely that the term vyāna was dropped and replaced with nāga. In turn, the original descriptions of the functions of the vital winds were further confused in the course of transmission.Now, the central focus is taught.Laksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!madhyalaksya@madhyalakṣya Within the mind, the focus shall be directed onto the light which is white coloured or yellow coloured or red coloured or grey coloured or blue coloured, like the flame of fire, like lightning, like the orb of the sun, like a half moon, appearing like flaming space, [and] of the same size as one's own body.Cf. shivayogapradipika 4.47cd–48: śṛṇuṣva madhyalakṣyaṃ ca kathitaṃ pūrvasūribhiḥ || 4.47 śvetādivarṇanavakhaṇḍacandrasaudāminīvahniśikhena bimbāt | jvalannabho vā sthalahīnam ekaṃ vilakṣayet tat khalu madhyalakṣyam 4.48 || ``(47cd) Hear now the central fixation which the ancient sages have taught. (48) One should focus on one [object] devoid of location or the burning space [emerging] from a sphere with flames and lightning shining (candra) into [all] nine landmasses (of the continent Jambūdvīpa: Bhārata, Hari, Kimpuruṣa, Ramyaka, Ramaṇa, Kuru, Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla and Ilāvṛta) in the colours of white etc. Truly, this is the central fixation.'' Despite all similarities, the differences of the techniques are: In the Śivayogapradīpikā, the practitioner should direct the mind towards the burning space or that which lacks locality. Conversely, Rāmacandra prescribes fixing one's mind onto the luminous mind, which is equated with the spatial extension of the human body.When this focus is practiced, the impurity within the mind is burned away. The sattva qualityFor a discussion of the guṇas in the context of Pātañjalayoga, see bryant2009.of the mind becomes manifest.The generation of the sattvic quality through the practice of madhyalakṣ(y)a also appears in sarvangayoga 3.28: madhya lakṣa mana madhya bicārai | vapu pramāna koi rūpa nihārai | yāte sātvik upajai āī | madhya lakṣa jo sādhai bhāī || ``The central focus directs the mind to reside at its centre, viewing the measure of the body according to its form. It produces the sattvic quality in those who practice it.''The person becomes blissful [and] remains like that.

div.head: [28. Divisions of space]
div.p: [XXVIII. Divisions of space]
div.note: Now, the divisions of space are taught.akasa@ākāśaThe advaya 7 (Ed. pp. 4–5) does not separate the practice of Madhyalakṣya from the five spaces. Here, both practices form a unified whole and follow a specific progression: atha madhyalakṣyalakṣaṇaṃ | prātaś citrādivarṇākhaṇḍasūryacakravat vahnijvālāvalīvat tadvihīnāntarikṣavat paśyati | tadākārākāritayā avatiṣṭhati | tadbhūyodarśanena guṇarahitākāśaṃ bhavati | visphurattārakākāradīpyamānagāḍhatamopamaṃ paramākāśaṃ bhavati | kālānalasamadyotamānaṃ mahākāśaṃ bhavati | sarvotkṛṣṭaparamadyutipradyotamānaṃ tattvākāśaṃ bhavati | koṭisūryaprakāśavaibhavasaṃkāśaṃ sūryākāśaṃ bhavati | evaṃ bāhyābhyantarasthavyomapañcakaṃ tārakalakṣyam | taddarśī vimuktaphalas tādṛgvyomasamāno bhavati | tasmāt tāraka eva lakṣyaṃ amanaskaphalapradaṃ bhavati || 7 || ``Now, he sees the characteristics of the central fixation [which is], like the indivisible orb of the sun, [being] colourful like the variety [of colours of the sun] in the early morning etc., [then] like a row of flames of fire, [and finally] the atmosphere devoid of that. He dwells in a state [in which he is mentally] assuming the form of the apparition of that. By contemplating that, the space (ākāśa) without qualities arises. [From that] supreme space (parākāśa) resembling absolute dense darkness shining in the form of a sparkling star arises. [From that] the great space (mahākāśa) whose shine equals the fire of time arises. [From that] the space of reality (tattvakāśa) arises, shining forth with supreme brilliance surpassing everything. [From that] the space of the sun (sūryākāśa) arises [which is endowed with] a brilliance as mighty as the brilliance of ten million suns. Thus, the fixations of Tāraka[yoga] consist of five spaces (vyoma) situated internally and externally. He who sees them becomes the same as such space [and] becomes one who is freed from the results [of his actions]. Because of that, only Tāraka[yoga] is the central fixation which bestows the fruits of the no mind state (amanaska).''Their foci are taught: Space,akasa@ākāśa beyond space,akasa@ākāśa!parakasa@parākāśa great space,akasa@ākāśa!mahakasa@mahākāśa reality space,akasa@ākāśa!tattvakasa@tattvākāśa the sun space.akasa@ākāśa!suryakasa@sūryākāśa The focus on space shall be visualised as pure and formless internally and externally. After that, the focus on beyond space shall be visualised as dense darknessInstead of extreme brightness as in the ssplonavla (Ed. p. 29) and advaya (Ed. p. 5), Rāmacandra has chosen to promote dense darkness in his parākāśa visualization.internally and externally. Then, the focus on the great space shall be visualised as the mass of the burning fire of the time of dissolution internally and externally. Afterwards, the focus on the reality space should be visualised internally and externally as resembling the splendour produced by the brightness of ten million lights. \flushpage

lg.tl: navacakraṃ\phantomsection navacakra°śloka navacakraṃ kalādhāraṃ \approx netratantra 7.1cd 2: ataḥ paraṃ pravakṣyāmi dhyānaṃ sūkṣmam anuttamam | ṛtucakraṃ svarādhāraṃ trilakṣyaṃ vyomapañcakam || granthidvādaśasaṃyuktaṃ śaktitrayasamanvitam | dhāmatrayapathākrāntaṃ nāḍītrayasamanvitam || \approx tantraloka 19.15: ṣoḍaśādhāraṣaṭcakralakṣyatrayakhapañcakāt | kvacid anyataratrātha prāguktapaśukarmavat | \approx manthana 25.2ab: ṣaṭcakraṃ ṣoḍaśādhāraṃ trilakṣyaṃ vyomapañcakam | \approx urmikaula 2.184: sarvaṃ samadhiyogena kulena hi tad ucyate | ṣaṭcakraṃ ṣoḍaśādhāraṃ trirlakṣaṃ vyomapañcakam || \approx SSP 2.31 (Ed. p. 43): navacakraṃ kalādhāraṃ trilakṣyaṃ vyomapañcakam | samyag etan na jānāti sa yogī nāmadhārakaḥ |= YSv (PT, p. 832) = YK 2.14: navacakraṃ kalādhāraṃ trilakṣaṃ vyomapañcakam | svadehe yo na jānāti sa yogī nāmadhārakaḥ | \approx YSv (PT, p. 839): navacakraṃ kalādhāraṃ dvilakṣaṃ vyomapañcakam | samagraṃ yo na jānāti sa yogī nāmadhārakaḥ | 2mm \approx yogatarangini quoted with reference Nityanāthapaddhati (Ed. p. 72) = hathatattvakaumudi 24.1: ṣaṭcakraṃ ṣoḍaśādhāraṃ dvilakṣyaṃ vyomapañcakam | svadehe ye na jānanti kathaṃ siddhyanti yoginaḥ | \approx PT (Ed. p. 172): ṣaṭcakraṃ ṣoḍaśādhāraṃ trilakṣaṃ vyomapañcakam | svadehe yo vijānāti sa guruḥ kathito budhaiḥ | \approx fausta1976 13 = Vivekāmartaṇḍa 6.3: ṣaṭcakraṃ ṣoḍaśādhāraṃ trailokyaṃ vyomapañcakam | svadehe ye na jānanti kathaṃ sidhyanti yoginaḥ | \approx mandalabrah 3.4.5: navacakraṃ ṣaḍādhāraṃ trilakṣyaṃ vyomapañcakam | samyag etan na jānāti sa yogī nāmato bhavet | \approx hathapradipika2024 4.61: ṣaṭcakraṃ ṣoḍaśādhāraṃ tridhā lakṣaṃ guṇatrayam | śeṣas tu granthavistāras trikūṭaṃ paramaṃ padam | 2mmtrilakṣyaṃ°lakṣaṃ vyomapañcakam/
samakriyāsvadehe yo na jānāti sa yogī nāmadhārakaḥ// 28.1 //

div.note: After that, the focus on sun space (sūryākāśa) shall be visualized as being accompanied by the shining disc of the sun internally and externally. From executing these foci, contact with diseases does not arise within the body. And, wrinkles, grey hair, sin, and merit do not arise.

28. 1 One who does not understand the full procedure [consisting of] the nine cakras,Rāmacandra’s ninefold cakra system is described in detail in 4–12, pp. –, and briefly repeated in 30, p. , in a different order for no clear reason.sixteen supports,The sixteen supports of Rāmacandra are the big toe support (pādāṅguṣṭhādhāra), root support (mūlādhāra), anus support (gudādhāra), penis support (liṅgādhāra), Udyāna[ support] (udyāna), navel support (nābhyādhāra), heart form support (hṛdayarūpādhāra), throat support (kaṇṭhādhāra), uvula support (ghaṇṭikādhāra), palate support (tālvādhāra), tongue support (jihvādhāra), teeth support (dantādhāra), nose support (nāsikādhāra), breath support at the root of the nose (nāsāmūle vāyvādhāra), centre of the eyebrows support support (bhrūvormadhyādhāra) and the eye support (netrādhāra). Each one of them is associated with a particular yogic technique. The sixteen supports are presented in Tattvayogabindu 31.the three foci,The three foci called antar(a)lakṣya, bahirlakṣya (often called bāhyalakṣya in the pañcalakṣya system of Rāmacandra and others) and madhyalakṣya are the predecessors of the five foci found in Tattvayogabindu, Yogasvarodaya as quoted in ramatosana and yogakarnika and sarvangayoga. The two additional foci are ūrdhvalakṣya and adholakṣya. A system of three foci is taught in tantralokatantralokax, manthana, netratantra, fausta1976, shivayogapradipika, ssplonavla, advaya, yogacudamani, mandalabrah. Structurally, it is surprising that Rāmacandra mentions all five lakṣyas in section 13, then teaches ūrdhvalakṣya in section 14 and adholakṣya in section 15, and just after the introduction of various other topics, he continues the subject of Lakṣyayoga by teaching bāhyalakṣya in section 23, antar(a)lakṣya in section 24 and finally madhyalakṣya in section 28.and five spaces is merely a yogin by name.As shown by the sources and testimonia on the previous page, the reception of the variants of this verse and its practices is widespread—from Śaiva Tantras such as tantraloka, manthana, and netratantra, through early and classical Haṭha and Rājayoga works (e.g. hathapradipika2024), into the post Haṭhapradīpikā era and the late yogaupaniṣaded. Most technical terms appear already in earlier Śaiva Tantras, such as the Mālinīvijayottaratantra, which, however, presents a more elaborate but conceptually distinct system of six lakṣyas (cf. vasudeva2004).\flushpage

div.head: [29. Sequence of cakras]
div.p: [XXIX. Sequence of cakras]
div.note: Now, the sequence of the cakras is taught.cakra@cakraRāmacandra again describes the cakras, briefly naming them—partly with different terms and locations than before. A detailed ninefold system was already given in 4–12; this repetition seems redundant. No parallel exists in the Yogasvarodaya, and in the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati only the positions, not the terminology, mostly coincide. No other ninefold cakra system known to me matches this terminology fully. It may thus be Rāmacandra’s own synthesis or based on an unknown source. For comparative overviews of nine , eight , and sixfold systems, see powell2023. For a tabular overview of the ninefold cakra systems and closely related systems with eight and six cakras see powell2023.At the base,In the previous section on cakras Rāmacandra situates the first cakra, which he there calls mūlacakra, at the beginning (ādau) [of supposedly the central channel], which should be at the anus if we assume an ascending order, cf. p. .there is the Brahmacakra.cakra@cakra!Brahmacakra@Brahmacakra Above the base at the root of the penis is the Svādiṣṭhānacakra.cakra@cakra!Svadhisthanacakra@Svādhiṣṭhānacakra At the navel, there is the Maṇipūrakacakra.cakra@cakra!Manipurakacakra@Maṇipūrakacakra In the heart [there is] the Anāhatacakra.cakra@cakra!Anahatacakra@Anāhatacakra Situated within the throat is the Viśuddhicakra.cakra@cakra!Visuddhicakra@Viśuddhicakra The sixth is the Tālucakra.cakra@cakra!Talucakra@Tālucakra In the centre of the eyebrows is the Ājñācakra.cakra@cakra!Ajnacakra@Ājñācakra At the aperture of BrahmanThe fontanelle, through which the vital principle of the yogi exits at death, cf. rootsofyoga2017.is the Kalācakra.cakra@cakra!Kalacakra@KalācakraThe term kalācakra (``cakra of the digit'') for the eighth cakra is unprecedented in other texts that teach cakra systems. A comparison of the term with the current standard collection of electronic texts in yogic and tantric studies, as well as with collections such as Muktabodha and GRETIL, yielded no hits. Thus, this appears to be an original and previously unknown term for a yogic cakra. All other texts that I am aware of designate the eighth cakra in a ninefold cakra system with different terms: peterson1888 4359/256.13, shivayogapradipika 3.15 and ssplonavla 2.8 call it nirvāṇacakram (``cakra of absolute extinction''); Yogasvarodaya as quoted in ramatosana (Ed. p. 833) just calls it aṣṭamaṃ cakraṃ (``the eighth cakra'') and siddhapuṃsaḥ sthalaṃ (``place of the accomplished human''); Rāmacandra himself in the previous chapter on cakras in section 11 picks this up and calls it aṣṭamacakraṃ (``eighth cakra'') and siddhapuruṣasya sthānaṃ (``place of the accomplished person''); saubhagya also calls it nirvāṇacakram, but provides us with yet another unique designation parabrahmacakram (``cakra of the supreme Brahman'').The ninth is the Ākāśacakra.cakra@cakra!Akasacakra@ĀkāśacakraThe term ākāśacakra for the ninth cakra in the known ninefold cakra systems occurs in shivayogapradipika 3.16 and ssplonavla 2.9 only.It is supreme emptiness. \flushpage

div.head: [30. Divisions of the wheels of support]
div.p: [XXX. Divisions of the wheels of support]
div.note: Now, the divisions of the groupI took cakra in the sense of ``group, crowd, totality'', cf. petersburger.of supportsadhara@ādhāraThe practice of sixteen ādhāras goes back to the yoga traditions of Śaivism and is mentioned in texts such as tantraloka, manthana and netratantra. The techniques were passed on, copied and recycled across the centuries among the yoga traditions of Haṭha and Rājayoga. Besides Rāmacandra's text, the other texts which present full lists of the sixteen ādhāras are Netroddyota commentary of Kṣemarāja on Netratantra 7.5; saradaavalon 25.24–25; shivayogapradipika 3.17–33; ssplonavla 2.10–25; yogatarangini 1.13 (Ed. p. 72–73) quotation with reference ``nityanāthapaddhatau'' (maybe another recension of the ssplonavla, see powell2023); hathatattvakaumudi 24.10–23 and 40.19; and jyotsna on hathapradipika2024, as well as ramatosana (Ed. p. 839–841) quotation with reference ``yogasvarodaye'' and yogakarnika quotation with reference ``yogasvarodaye'' 14–36. Haṭhasaṃketacandrikā (cf. GOML R3239, f. 201 l. 20 to f. 204 ll. 5–6) directly quotes the Tattvayogabindu without reference. Comparing the various lists of ādhāras reveals great variability. Rāmacandra's system draws from the Yogasvarodaya and the ssplonavla. When there are differences in the descriptions of the respective ādhāras among the texts I note them in the annotations without providing a reference again; for the Sanskrit, see the above provided references.is taught.1.5em As a result of focusing on a light at the big toes of both feet, the gaze becomes steady.In all previously mentioned systems, the big toe is the first ādhāra. In most texts, the practitioner is instructed to fix the mind onto the big toe either one shall visualize a light there (as in shivayogapradipika) or the light is already present. The saradaavalon, however, instructs to fix prāṇa in each ādhāra listed. Here, the practice of the ādhāras is subsumed under the dhāraṇā limb of an eight fold (aṣṭāṅga) yoga system.1.5em The root supportadhara@ādhāra!muladhara@mūlādhāra is the second [one]. The heel of the back foot is placed at the base of the big toe of the foot.The base of the big toe of the foot (pādasyāṅguṣṭhamūla) is probably the big toe joint of the foot or articulatio metatarsophalangealis hallucis.The fire is strengthened. [In other words,] one heel is placed at the root support. The heel of the other foot is placed at the base of the big toe of this foot. The fire is kindled.Rāmacandra combines the techniques presented in YSv and SSP for this ādhāra, resulting in a siddhāsana like bodily position.Netroddyota, saradaavalon and jyotsna give the ankle (gulpha) as the second ādhāra.\flushpage

div.note: 1.5em The third is the place of the anus support.adhara@ādhāra!gudadhara@gudādhāraNetroddyota, saradaavalon and jyotsna provide the knee (jānu) as the third ādhāra.As a result of expansion, contraction and compression, the vital wind becomes stable [on it]. And then, the person does not die. 1.5em The fourth is the penis support.adhara@ādhāra!lingadhara@liṅgādhāra As a result of the practice of contracting the penis in the middle of the [support], the adamantine channel (i.e., central channel)nadi@nāḍī!vajranadi@vajranāḍīThe adamantine channel (vajranāḍī) is another synonym for the central channel. Rāmacandra adapted the term from the Yogasvarodaya. yogatarangini in the commentary on 1.13 uses the term vajragarbha (``adamantine womb'').arises in the posterior staff (i.e., spine).The posterior staff (paścimadaṇḍa) is the spine. Cf. peterson1888 4365.From the repeated practice, both breath and mind enter it. As a result of the transition of both [breath and mind] the trinity of knotsThe trinity of knots are: 1. the knot of Brahmā (brahmagranthi)granthi@granthi!brahmagranthi@brahmagranthi is situated in the lower regions of the body (cf. liersch2026 23–24); 2. the knot of Viṣṇu (viṣṇugranthi)granthi@granthi!visnugranthi@viṣṇugranthi at the level of the heart (cf. liersch2026 25 and gsatacod 80); and 3. the knot of Rudra (rudragranthi)granthi@granthi!rudragranthi@rudragranthi at the level of the head or between the eyebrows (cf. liersch2026 25 and gsatacod 81). Depending on text and tradition, it is either the breath (cf. asiddhi 13.9–11) or the kuṇḍalinī (cf. yogabija 96–97 and gsatacod 74–86) that enters the central channel and pierces the knots. gsatacod 48 states that the entrance to the central channel is blocked by phlegm and that the three knots have arisen from the three guṇas. They obstruct the central passage.within [the central channel] is pierced. Because of the piercing of those [knots], the breath becomes full in Brahmā's lotus and remains there.Brahman's lotus refers to the eighth cakra in Rāmacandra's system, cf. chapter 8, p. . The same location is expressed in the ssplonavla 2.13 and yogatarangini commentary on 1.13 with the term brahmaraguhā (``buzzing hive'') situated on top of the head (jogpradipyaka 932; also cf. peterson1888 4366 and gorakbhani 28.2 and 30.4).As a result of that, the stopping of semen arises.Breath, mind and semen are interconnected. If one of them stops its movement, all stop their movement, cf. asiddhi 7.19–20 and 23.The person becomes youthful forever.Most of the consulted texts situate the fourth ādhāra at the penis (meḍhra). saradaavalon and jyotsna place the fourth support at the thighs (ūru). shivayogapradipika 3.20 and ssplonavla 2.13 additionally associate the practice with the arrest of semen (bindustambha). However, ssplonavla calls this vajrolī.\flushpage

div.note: 1.5em The fifth is Uḍḍīyāṇaadhara@ādhāra!Uddiyana@Uḍḍīyāṇa,For a discussion of the term uḍḍīyāṇa, see p. n. .that is, Svādhiṣṭhānaadhara@ādhāra!Svadhisthana@Svādhiṣṭhāna. As a result of performing a lock at that place, faeces and urine disappear.shivayogapradipika, ssplonavla and yogatarangini share the concept of binding at Uḍḍīyāna. hathatattvakaumudi instructs to do a pressing (moṭana) at the waist (kaṭau). Netroddyota, along with saradaavalon and jyotsna situate the fifth ādhāra at the anus (pāyu or sīvanī). The Yogasvarodaya situates the fifth ādhāra at the belly (jaṭharādhāra).1.5em The sixth is the support of the navel.adhara@ādhāra!nabhyadhara@nābhyādhāra There, from the repeated practice of praṇavapranava@praṇava,The syllable oṃ. See bryant2009 2009, pp. 105–109 and harimoto2014 2014, pp. 151–163 for a more detailed discussion of the term praṇava in the context of the Pātañjalayogaśāstra.the unstruck soundnada@nādaCf. hathapradipika2024 4.17 et seqq.arises by itself.ssplonavla prescribes reciting oṃ at the navel; yogatarangini adds meditation on the form of consciousness (cidrūpa); and hathatattvakaumudi instructs retaining the breath at the navel, causing the sound of oṃ to rise into emptiness. In the Yogasvarodaya, breath retention at the navel likewise produces spontaneous nāda, while the shivayogapradipika directs contemplation of Kuṇḍalinī there. The Netroddyota identifies the kanda as the sixth support.1.5em The seventh is the support in the form of the heart.adhara@ādhāra!hrdayadhara@hṛdayādhāra The six lotuses [become] upward facing [and] open up as a result of the restraint of the breath in this location.Rāmacandra's mention of ṣaḍ api kamalāny (``six lotuses'') seems inconsistent, as he previously (section 29) taught a ninefold cakra system. In the ssplonavla, Yogasvarodaya, and yogatarangini, practice at the seventh ādhāra culminates in the blossoming of the heart lotus alone; in the hathatattvakaumudi, it is consciousness that blossoms in the heart. The shivayogapradipika describes the heart centre as a downward facing eight petaled lotus bestowing desires, where one should place the mind in the pericarp (karṇikā) as a liṅga of light. Netroddyota identifies the seventh ādhāra as the nāḍī, the middle path between navel and heart (nābhihṛnmadhyamārge tu sarvakāmābhidho mataḥ |), while saradaavalon and jyotsna list the navel as the seventh.1.5em The eighth is the throat support.adhara@ādhāra!kanthadhara@kaṇṭhādhāra There, the Jālandhara lockbandha@bandha!Jalandhara@JālandharaThis passage shows how Rāmacandra shifts between his two sources. In chapter~11, he places Jālandhara at the brahmarandhra; see p.~ for a discussion.is performed. When [the lock] is engaged, the breath in the Iḍānadi@nāḍī!Ida@Iḍā [and] Piṅgalānadi@nāḍī!Pingala@Piṅgalā channels becomes firm.The Netroddyota locates the support in the belly (jaṭhara), while the saradaavalon and jyotsna place the eighth support in the heart. The remaining texts agree in this regard.

div.note: 1.5em The ninth is the support of the uvula. The tip of the tongue becomes attached to it. As a result of that, the nectar of immortality flows from the immortality digit. From drinking the nectar of immortality, diseases do not spread in the body.Most texts with the sixteen ādhāra system share this concept. Only saradaavalon and jyotsna situate the ninth support at the neck (grīva), and Netroddyota at the heart.1.5em The tenth is the support of the palate. After the moving and milking have been done, [and] after abiding at the entrance with the tongue in the middle of it, the tongue resides inserted within the [cavity above the] palate.The ninth, tenth, eleventh and twelfth supports are all associated with the tongue related haṭhayogic khecarīmudrā and its forerunners. For a detailed account of this khecarīmudrā, see mallinson2010. Netroddyota places the tenth support at the tortoise channel (kūrmanāḍī), whereas saradaavalon and jyotsna situate it at the throat (kaṇṭha).1.5em The eleventh is the tongue support at the surface of the tongue.adhara@ādhāra!jihvadhara@jihvādhāra In the middle of that [support], the tip of the tongue is churned.For a discussion of the term manthana in the context of khecarīmudrā, see mallinson2010.When that has been done, a very sweet liquid oozes out. Moreover, after that, the knowledge of areas like poetry, singing, metrics and dance is generated.Almost all texts teaching the sixteen ādhāras share the concept of the churning of the tongue with only minor differences: ssplonavla teaches the destruction of all diseases (sarvaroganāśa) as the result of this practice, yogatarangini calls the practice jihvādhobhāgādhāra. The Netroddyota alone teaches the throat (kaṇṭha) as the eleventh ādhāra. Here, it states: lambhikasya sthitaś cordhve sudhādhāraḥ sudhātmakaḥ || ``Above the place of the uvula is a stream of nectar resembling nectar itself.''.

div.note: 1.5em Above that is the twelfth, the tooth support within the two [top front] teeth.adhara@ādhāra!dantadhara@dantādhāraSSP 2.21 (Ed. p. 36) teaches the brows as the twelfth ādhāra. Rāmacandra follows the YSv here. Given the other descriptions, it is apparent that Rāmacandra switched between both sources when compiling the section on the sixteen ādhāras.At this place, the tip of the tongue is to be positioned with force for the duration of one ghaṭi or half a ghaṭi.One ghaṭi equals 1/60 of a day (see sircar1966), which is 24 minutes. Half a ghaṭi would thus equal 12 minutes.Abiding therein, all the practitioner's diseases will disappear.Most of the texts teach a practice that involves contact between the tongue and the teeth. Rāmacandra and Yogasvarodaya teach to push the tongue forcefully against the [upper] teeth. shivayogapradipika instructs to rub the tip of the tongue at the upper teeth for half a year, which would cause the practitioner to see an inner light. hathatattvakaumudi mixes the two previous ideas. The name of the twelfth ādhāra here is dvijādhāra, and Sundaradeva also calls it rājadanta. The yogin presses the tip of the tongue against this point, and hence, he perceives an inner light within six months. yogatarangini surprisingly teaches the same technique as Rāmacandra and not the bhrūmadhyādhāra of ssplonavla. Netroddyota names the palate as the twelfth support and lets us know that at the root of it is that which is blissful, which is enveloped by the somakalā. saradaavalon and jyotsna list the nose as the twelth support.1.5em The thirteenth is the support of the nose. When that is set as the focus, the mind becomes stable.The majority of texts teach either the nose, the base of the nose as in shivayogapradipika (ghrāṇamūla) and hathatattvakaumudi (ghrāṇapada), or the tip of the nose (nāsāgra) as the ssplonavla and yogatarangini. Whereas Netroddyota, saradaavalon and jyotsna teach the place in between the brows as the thirteenth ādhāra.1.5em The fourteenth is the support of the vital wind at the bridge of the nose.adhara@ādhāra!nasamulavayvadhara@nāsāmūle vāyvādhāra As a result of stabilising the gaze therein, one's own brilliance becomes apparent within six months. When the brilliance has manifested the entire mundane bond breaks.Yogasvarodaya and ssplonavla provide the term kapāṭādhāra. yogatarangini teaches the base of the nose as the fourteenth ādhāra. All other texts teach fixing the mind and the breath at the forehead. Netroddyota calls this place at the forehead ``a wish fulfilling jewel with its abode at the crossroads of the four channels'' (cintāmaṇyabhidhānākhyaś catuṣpathanivāsi yat).\flushpage

YSv (PT, pp. 840–41): netrādhāraḥ ṣoḍaśo 'yam (aṅgulyagre na YK 2.36) aṅgulyagreṇa cālayet | pṛthvīmadhye tu yat kiñcid varttate (sarvajñaḥ prabhavas tena varddhate YK 2.36) jaṭharānalaḥ | pratyakṣaṃ tad bhavet sarvaṃ tad ābhyāsān na saṃśayaḥ |cf. SSP 2.25 (Ed. p. 37): avaśiṣṭe ṣoḍaśe brahmarandhram ākāśacakram | tatra śrīgurucaraṇāmbujayugmaṃ sadāvalokayet | ākāśavat pūrṇo bhavati | \approx hathasamketacandrikajodhpur (MMPP 2244, f. 99r l. 4): atha ṣoḍaśo netrādhāraḥ 16 ayaṃ aṃgulyagreṇa cālyate tadābhyāsāt pṛthivīmadhye yat kiñcit tejo vartate | tat sarvaṃ tejo dṛṣṭiviṣayaṃ bhavati | taddarśanāt puruṣaḥ sarvajño bhavati | iti pūrvoktaṣoḍaśādhārāṇāṃ spaṣṭo 'rthaḥ |ṣoḍaśoṣoḍaśaḥ netrādhāraḥne ādhāraḥnetrā/ ayam aayaṃṅgulyagreṇaaṃgugreṇaagulyagreṇa cālyate/ tadabhyāsāt pṛthvīpṛthivī°madhye yatkiṃcit tejotejaḥom. vartatevatate/ tatsarvatejotatsarvaṃ tejotatsarvaṃ tajaso dṛṣṭidṛṣṭī°viṣayaṃ bhavatibhavatī/ taddarśanāt putaddarśanaḥtatdarśaḥtadarśanātruṣaḥ sarvajño bhavatibhavatī//

div.note: 1.5em The fifteenth support is situated in the middle of the eyebrows.adhara@ādhāra!bhrumadhyadhara@bhrūmadhyādhāra As a result of stabilising the gaze therein, ten million rays of light sparkle.shivayogapradipika teaches gazing above the brows, which quickly brings about the appearance of light. ssplonavla calls it the ``support of the forehead'' (lalāṭādhāra), in which the practitioner shall visualize a cluster of light. yogatarangini teaches the centre of the brows. By concentrating on this point, a direct vision of many rayed light occurs, and one’s mind will merge into the sun sky (etasya dṛḍhābhyāse sūryākāśo līyate |). hathatattvakaumudi calls it the ``support of ether'' (vyomādhāra) and explains that by gazing at it, everything is perceived as light. However, Netratantra teaches the brahmarandhra as the fifteenth support. Netroddyota declares it as the ``support of the fourth state'' (turyādhāra). saradaavalon and jyotsna also teach the top of the head (mūrdhan) as the fifteenth.1.5em The sixteenth is the eye support.adhara@ādhāra!netradhara@netrādhāra It is caused to be rubbed with the fingertips. As a result of that practice, some light arises from the earth[ element].Perhaps, tejas arises from pṛthvī, because its origin is unknown and in Śaiva Tantras the earth as the bottom tattva contains the entire brahmāṇḍa, cf. tantrika3.That entire light becomes the object of vision. As a result of seeing that, the person becomes omniscient.Rāmacandra's description of netrādhāra is very similar to yogatarangini, which also instructs the yogin to rub the eyes with the fingers in order to generate the perception of a light. Other texts have some noteworthy differences: shivayogapradipika teaches to fix [the gaze] above the eyes. Due to that, the yogin sees a mass of light at the corner of his eyes. hathatattvakaumudi teaches to meditate upon the eyes. By seeing a mass of light at the corner of the eyes, one soon becomes like Śiva. ssplonavla teaches to visualize the pair of lotus feet of the revered teacher (śrīgurucaraṇāmbujayugmaṃ) at the brahmarandhra in which the ākāśacakra is situated. The jyotsna, too, lists the brahmarandhra. saradaavalonavalon and Netratantra teach the dvādaśānta as the sixteenth support. tantrika3, p. 210. Netroddyota explains: nāḍyādhāraḥ paraḥ sūkṣmo ghanavyāptiprabodhakaḥ || ``The support of the [central?] channel is the highest subtle one which awakens complete pervasion.''\flushpage

[31. Reflection of Aṣṭāṅgayoga]\phantomsection
[XXXI. Reflection of Aṣṭāṅgayoga] Now, the reflection of AṣṭāṅgayogaAstangayoga@AṣṭāṅgayogaGiven the extensive list of fifteen yogas presented at the beginning of this text does not contain aṣṭāṅgayoga, one wonders why this type of yoga suddenly appears and why it was not included within the list of methods of Rājayoga. Suffice it to say that he followed the structure of his main source text. A comparative analysis of the integration of Aṣṭāṅgayoga into the early modern complex yoga taxonomies can be found on p. .is explained: observancesyama@yama, restrictionsniyama@niyama, postureasana@āsana, breath controlpranayama@prāṇāyāma, withdrawal of the sensespratyahara@pratyāhāra, meditationdhyana@dhyāna, concentrationdharana@dhāraṇāThe reversed order of the sixth (dhāraṇā) and seventh (dhyāna) limb of the ``classical'' Pātañjalayoga model is striking (cf. Pātañjalayogaśāstra 2.29). Rāmacandra's main source text, the Yogasvarodaya, names aṣṭāṅgayoga but does not list dhyāna in the respective verse (cf. sources). The critical edition of the Lonavla Yoga Institute of ssplonavla mentions two manuscripts (J1 and J2) with Rāmacandra's order. According to vasudeva2004, this reversed order frequently appears in yoga texts structured in ṣaḍaṅga or even pañcāṅga systems. It is found in Jayākhyasaṃhitā and Maitrāyaṇīyopaniṣad. Furthermore, it is present in the Śaiva Rauravatantra, Kiraṇatantra, Mataṅgatantra, as well as in Buddhist Tantras like the Guhyasamājatantra and Kālacakratantra. Vāyupurāṇa teaches this ``reversed'' order in its pañcāṅga schema. powell2023 mentions that he has not found an Aṣṭāṅgayoga system with dhyāna and dhāraṇā reversed outside of the shivayogapradipika 2.1–9. Some witnesses of ssplonavla, Tattvayogabindu and implicitly the Yogasvarodaya as quoted in ramatosana and yogakarnika can be added to this group. It appears that the source for this concept goes back to the Vīraśaiva milieu of the fifteenth century. For a useful table of the texts, including the reversed order, see powell2023.\phantomsection and absorptionsamadhi@samādhi. Their characteristics are taught. 1.5em Peace, mastery of the six senses,The sixth sense is the mental faculty (manas or citta), cf. white2021.little food, the conquest of sleep, the conquest of cold, [and] the conquest of heat.Rāmacandra presents a unique mix of his two primary sources: Yogasvarodaya lists peace (śānti), contentment (santoṣa), little sleep (nidrālpa), taming of the mind (manaso dama) and \ldots These are the observances. 1.5em Now, the restrictions: the mind is to be restrained from the unsteady state [and] caused to be grounded in tranquillity, dwelling in a lonely place, maintaining equanimity towards all kinds of living beings, indifference, one shall not desire any object, contentment with whatever is obtained, never forgetting the name of the highest lord, [and] one shall not indulge in self pity. These are the restrictions.

SSP 2.38 (Ed. p. 46): atha dhyānam | asti kaścana paramādvaitasya bhāvaḥ | sa evātmeti yathā yad yat sphurati tattatsvarūpam eveti bhāvayet | sarvabhūteṣu samadṛṣṭiś ca | iti dhyānalakṣaṇam |dhyānaṃom. caom. bahutaraṃom. prāg uom.ktaṃuktam |uktam tenātratena atra nocyate\phantomsection na ucyate//

div.note: 2.2ememptiness of the inner organ (śūnyāntaḥkaraṇa). ssplonavla lists: tranquillity (upaśama), mastery of all senses (sarvendriyajaya), and conquest of food, sleep, cold, wind, heat (ahāranidrāśītavātātapajaya). 1.5em The characteristic of posture has been discussed in many works. For that reason, it is not discussed here. 1.5em Young persons cannot practise breath controlpranayama@prāṇāyāma. That is why it is just mentioned by name.It is crucial to note here that Yogasvarodaya states that young persons are not qualified to practice posture and breath control, but that, by the power of great merit a great soul becomes capable, cf. yogakarnika quoted with reference yogasvarodaye 7.2 (āsane prāṇasaṃyāme na śaktāḥ sukumārakāḥ | mahāpuṇyaprabhāveṇa śakyate tu mahātmanā |). Right after that statement, the text continues to present detailed instructions for eight kumbhakas, cf. yogakarnika quoted with reference yogasvarodaye 7.3–10, 7.23–24 and 7.68–72. The whole extent of Yogasvarodaya's teaching on prāṇāyāma cannot be determined since it is absent in the quotes of ramatosana and is just partially quoted in yogakarnika. It seems that Rāmacandra, who previously strictly followed the structure of the Yogasvarodaya, consciously decided to exclude these teachings for the reason he gives here. Therefore, he probably directly alludes to part of his audience: sukumāras, young persons, or, considering all previous allusions to a wealthy and royal lifestyle, young courtiers and princes.1.5em Withdrawal of the sensespratyahara@pratyāhāra is taught. The mind is supposed to be turned away from cyclic existence and caused to abide in the self. The changes that arise within the mind should also be restrained. An intellect that is capable of creating many wonders arises. This is to be kept secret. 1.5em Meditationdhyana@dhyāna has been taught many times before [in this text]. Because of that, it is not discussed here.Rāmacandra perhaps refers to the teaching of the nine cakras and other sections of the text in which meditation is mentioned. The same schema is already found in the dhyāna descriptions of Śivayogapradīpika 3.4–33, cf. powell2023. He might also hint at the various methods he subsumes under Lakṣayoga. Most likely, Rāmacandra consciously decided to skip a description of samādhi, since ramatosana quoted with reference Yogasvarodaye (Ed. p. 841) defines samādhi as follows: samādhir niścalā buddhiḥ śvāsocchvāsādivarjitaḥ | ``Samādhi is the immovable intellect devoid of inhalation, exhalation, etc.''. If, indeed, one purpose of Rāmacandra's text was to teach Rājayoga to young courtiers or princes, surely children would not be taught that the highest level of yoga is accomplished by stopping breathing altogether.\phantomsection \flushpage

div.head: [32. Identity of the universe and the body]
div.p: [XXXII. Identity of the universe and the body]
div.note: Now, there is the identity of the universebrahmanda@brahmāṇḍa and the body.pinda@piṇḍaThe concept of the body as a microcosmic manifestation of a macrocosmic universe is a common feature in yogic literature, see rootsofyoga2017.Because of that, the objects that exist in the universe are also in the body. They are taught. 1.5em Talaloka@loka!Tala@Tala exists at the base of the big toe[s] of the feet. On top of the feet exists Talātala.loka@loka!Talatala@Talātala Mahātalaloka@loka!Mahatala@Mahātala exists at the ankles.A description of rasātala is missing in the Tattvayogabindu. Either this item in the enumeration was lost in transmission or we must assume an authorial mistake. A phrase like ``gulphopari rasātalaṃ vartate |'' would be expected at this point of the text. Both source texts Rāmacandra used describe rasātala right after the description of mahātala.Sutalaloka@loka!Sutala@Sutala exists within the lower leg. Vitalaloka@loka!Vitala@Vitala exists within the knees. Atalaloka@loka!Atala@Atala exists within the two thighs.Hindu cosmography, as described in various Purāṇas, the Atharvaveda, etc., assumes fourteen worlds (lokas), seven higher ones (vyāhṛtis) and seven lower ones (pātālas). The higher lokas (1–7) are described as the heavens, populated by mortals, celestial or divine beings, gods and higher gods, and full of truth. The lower lokas (8–14), which are here mapped onto the human body, constitute the different ``hells'' and are the abode of the nāgas or serpents and demons, cf. haag2012. According to Patañjali in his bhāṣya on Yogasūtra 3.26,yogasutra the beings residing in their respective lokas experience the fruit of their karma. Residence in those abodes, however, is never eternal but lasts until the particular individual's karma has been exhausted and has borne its due fruit (bryant2009). A well known depiction that shows the mapping of the lokas onto the body is Viṣṇu Viśvarūpa, India, Rajasthan, Jaipur, ca. 1800–1820 in the Victoria and Albert Museum, see p. . Directly related to the Tattvayogabindu is the depiction of a Siddha's body that shows the equivalence of the self and the universe in the manuscript of ssplonavla located in Mehragarh Museum Jodhpur, see p. .\flushpage

The two Nepalese manuscripts N1 and N2 exhibit a substantial lacuna, which suggests their close affiliation. They must both be derived from the same exemplar or from each other. div.head: [33. Triad of worlds]
div.p: [XXXIII. Triad of worlds]
div.note: Now, the triad of worlds within the body is taught.The earliest conception of the equation of the cosmos with the body is found in rigveda 10,90. This concept becomes linked with yogic practice in subsequent Hindu traditions. According to the Bhagavadgītā and the Kūrma Purāṇa, the deities Viṣṇu and Śiva are described as engaging in the practice of yoga. During this practice, they assimilate all external aspects by either encompassing the entire universe within their cosmic bodies or by engulfing everything, see white2011. For a detailed exposition of the Purāṇic concept of the universe in Patañjali's yoga, see the commentaries on yogasutra 3.25, e.g., yogasutra or bryant2009. The idea of situating the universe into the yogic body is carried forward into the traditions of Haṭha and Rājayoga and becomes a substantial constituent of their worldview, cf. asiddhi 15–19. For a collection of references to the yogic body, see rootsofyoga2017 2017: 171–227.The earth realm (bhūrloka)loka@loka!Bhurloka@bhūrloka is situated at the root support (mūlādhāra). The atmosphere (bhuvarloka)loka@loka!Bhuvarloka@bhuvarloka is at the tip of the penis. Heaven (svarloka)loka@loka!Svarloka@svarloka is at the base of the penis.

div.head: [34. Upper tetrad of worlds]
div.p: [XXXIV. Upper tetrad of worlds]
div.note: Now, the upper tetrad of worlds is taught. The world of greatness (maharloka)loka@loka!Maharloka@maharloka is located at the sprout of the staff of the back. The world of men (janaloka)loka@loka!Janaloka@janaloka is within the opening of the spine.The localisation of the upper tetrad of worlds occurs along the spine, which is imagined as a lotus. While the Tattvayogabindu and the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati locate maharloka at the sprout (°aṅkūre) of the spine, in the Yogasvarodaya we read about the root (°mūle) of the spine. The next world janaloka is at the opening (°chidra°) of the spine. In the context of the comparison of the spine to a lotus, this must be the rhizome of the lotus because the tube of the stem grows from it. I want to thank mallinson2007 for this hint. This rhizome is likely the root bulb mentioned in Tattvayogabindu 3, from which the central channel emerges. The satyaloka within the lotus of the spine may be the lotus of the eighth or ninth cakra (section 11–12).In the centre of the tube of that spine is the world of ascetic heat (tapoloka)loka@loka!Tapoloka@tapoloka. Within the lotus of the spine is the world of truth (satyaloka)loka@loka!Satyaloka@satyaloka.For extensive accounts of Hindu cosmography and the inhabitants of the various spheres of the cosmos, see kirfel1954's study of Purāṇic cosmography, bhagavata 5.16 26, and, more generally, kirfel1927's kirfel1927.\flushpage

div.head: [35. Lords of the world]
div.p: [XXXV. Lords of the world]
div.note: Now, there are four lords (1–4) of the worldslokasvamin@lokasvāmin in the universe.Only the reading of D, J, K1 and U1 (\beta group) is plausible and lectio dificilior. The source text confirms this; the Yogasvarodaya introduces the lokapālakāḥ, which Rāmacandra renders as lokasvāminaḥ. In the \gamma group, the subject was not understood and rewritten in an attempt to fix the passage.They also exist in the body. [Other deities and worlds exist within the body]I decided to add the words in the square brackets to derive the most probable sense of the list of locations based on the source texts.two in the belly (5–6), two in the thighs (7–8), at the location of the chest (9), at the pit of the throat (10), in the centre of the throat (11), at the root of the uvula (12), at the entrance of the palate (13), at the forehead (14),\ldots Rāmacandra greatly simplifies his source texts at this point. The parallel passages in the Yogasvarodaya and the ssplonavla provide much more detail. The background of what Rāmacandra wants to express lies somewhere between the two sources available to him (see sources in the first layer of the apparatus criticus). I translate the respective passage in the ramatosana quoted with reference Yogasvarodaye (Ed. p. 842 ) as follows: ``There are now four world world guardians amid the external universe. Having recognised these within the body, the supreme ruler (of the body?) may be fully successful. Indra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa are the deities of the body (ātman). (1) In the four petalled Mūlādhāra [cakra] is the great one who is seated on an elephant (Indra). (2) There at Svādiṣṭhāna is the Creator, the great Hari (Viṣṇu). (3) In the Maṇipūra is the one with the trident in hand, the great lord of the eight supernatural powers (Śiva). (4) at the gate of the palate, (5) amid the palate, (6) on the forehead, (7) in the chest and (8) throat, (9) at the junction in the skull, and at (10) the uvula, (11) as well as at the opening of Brahman and (20) at the nine cakras, upper cakra and (21) at the triple peak. They are in the 21 worlds and must be realised in detail.'' The passage of ssplonavla 3.4–5 reveals further details of the physical locations listed by Rāmacandra: ``Thus, Brahmā is the deity within the fourfold world. He resides in the body in various forms of self esteem and pride. The world of Viṣṇu is situated in the belly (kukṣau). Viṣṇu is the deity there. In the body, he manifests as the performer of various forms of activity. In the heart is the world of Rudra. Rudra is the deity there. Within the body, he resides in the form of strength. In the location of the chest (vakṣaḥsthale) is the world of Īśvara. Īśvara is the deity there. Within the body, he exists in the form of contentment. At the root of the throat (kaṇṭhamūle) is the world of Sadāśiva. Sadāśiva is the deity there. Within the body, he exists in the form of being\ldots \flushpage

div.p: cf. YSv (PT, p. 842): śṛṅgāṭikā kapāle ca lambikā brahmarandhrake | navacakram ūrddhvacakrañ ca trikūṭety ekaviṃśatiḥ | brahmāṇḍāni vasantīti jñātavyāni prayatnataḥ |cf. SSP 3.4–5 (Ed. pp. 52–53): śṛṅgāṭe kulalokaḥ | tatra kuleśvaro devatā | piṇḍamadhya ānandasvarūpī tiṣṭhati | śaṅkhamadhye nalinīsthāne 'kuleśalokaḥ | tatra akuleśvaro devatā | piṇḍamadhye nirabhimānāvasthā tiṣṭhati | brahmarandhre parabrahmalokaḥ | tatra parabrahma devatā | piṇḍamadhye paripūrṇadaśā tiṣṭhati | ūrdhvakamale parāparalokaḥ | tatra parameśvaro devatā | piṇḍamadhye parāparabhāvas tiṣṭhati | trikūṭasthāne śaktilokaḥ | tatra parāśaktir devatā | piṇḍamadhye 'sti vāvasthā sarvāsāṃ sarvakartṛtvāvasthā tiṣṭhati | evaṃ piṇḍamadhye saptapātālasahitaikaviṃśatibrahmāṇḍasthānavicāraḥ |śṛṅgāṭikāyāmśṛgāṭikāyāṃśṛṃgāṭikā// kapālamadhyekarālamadhyekapolamadhye// kamalinīmadhyekamalinīmadhyaṃ// brahmarandhrebrahmaraṃdhraṃbrahmaraṃdhra°// ūrdhvakamalinyāṃ tri:kūṭasthāneūrdhvakamalinyaḥ || trikūṭasthāne || saptapātāleūrdhvakamalinyāḥ || trikūṭasthāne | saptapātāleurdhvakamalinyaḥ trikūṭasthāneūrdhvaṃ kamalīnyā trikūṭasthānamurdhvakamalinyās trikūṭasthānamkamalinyas trikūṭasthānamkamalīnyāṃ strikūṭasthānam// evam eom.ekamkaviṃśasthāneṣv eekaviṃśatisthāneom.ekaviṃśasthānekaṃ viṃśasthāneṣvekaṃ viṃśasthānek°kaviṃśatibrahmāṇḍāniekaviṃśatibrahmāḍāniekaviṃśabrahmāniekaviṃśabrahmāṇḍāniekaviṃśabrahmāḍānī vasantivasaṃtī//
